- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] \label{proof:consistency} We begin by defining a  proper metric space. By \cref{assump:Lip_and_bounded}, all random variables are bounded. Suppose that $ \max_{i,j}\{\| V_{i} \| _{\infty} ,\| U_{j} \| _{\infty}\} \leqslant K$. A canonical causal model $ \mathcal{M} \in \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{G} ,\mathcal{F} ,\boldsymbol{U})$ is decided by  \begin{equation*} \theta _{\mathcal{M}} =( f_{1} ,\cdots ,f_{n_{V}} ,{P}({U_{1}}) ,\cdots , {P}({U_{n_{U}}})) , \end{equation*} where $ f_{i}$ are functions in the structure equations (\ref{eq:structure_equation}) and $ U_{j}$ are uniform parts of the latent variables. We denote $ \mathcal{M}^{\theta }$ to be the SCM represented by $ \theta $, the underlying SCM be $ \mathcal{M}^{\theta^*}$ and $P^\theta$  to be the distribution of $ \mathcal{M}^\theta$. We consider the space \[ M=\mathcal F_{V_1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal F_{V_{n_V}}\times\prod_{j=1}^{n_U}\mathcal P([-K,K]^{d_j^U}), \] where \[ \mathcal F_{V_i}=\begin{cases} \mathcal F_{\hat L_f}^K([-K,K]^{d_{i,\text{in}}^V},[-K,K]^{d_{i,\text{out}}^V}),&V_i\text{ continuous},\\ \{p:[-K,K]^{d_{i,\text{in}}^V}\rightarrow\Delta_{n_i}:\operatorname{Lip}(p)\leqslant\hat L_f\},&V_i\text{ categorical}. \end{cases} \] Here $d_{i,\text{in}}^V,d_{i,\text{out}}^V$ are the input and output dimensions of $f_i$, $\mathcal F_{\hat L_f}^K$ has uniform output $1$-norm bound $K$ and common Lipschitz bound $\hat L_f$, and $\mathcal P(A)$ denotes the probability measures on $A$. For $ \theta  =\left( f_{1} ,\cdots ,f_{n_{V}} ,{P}({U_{1}}) ,\cdots , {P}({U_{n_{U}}})\right) ,\theta' =\left( f_{1}' ,\cdots ,f_{n_{V}}' ,{P}({U_{1}'}) ,\cdots ,{P}({U_{n_{U}}'})\right)$, we define a metric on $ M$ \begin{equation*} d( \theta  ,\theta') =\sum _{k=1}^{n_{V}} \| f_{k} -f_{k}' \| _{\infty } +\sum _{k=1}^{n_{U}} W(P(U_{k}),{P}({U_{k}'})) . \end{equation*} We derive the population continuity bound in the fixed dimensions of this theorem. Couple corresponding non-Gumbel latent laws optimally and take the product of these couplings, using their independence. The expected joint latent $1$-norm discrepancy is the sum of their marginal Wasserstein distances. Generate the observed nodes in a topological order. At a continuous node the expected output discrepancy is at most the structural output $1$-norm approximation error plus $\hat L_f$ times the expected input discrepancy. At a categorical node with conditional propensity vectors $p,p'$, a maximal coupling has disagreement probability $\|p-p'\|_1/2$; its expected label distance is at most $(n_i-1)\|p-p'\|_1/2$. Such a coupling assigns common mass $\min\{p_k,p'_k\}$ to label $k$ and distributes the remaining masses on the disjoint residual supports. It preserves each model's conditional categorical law. If $e$ is the sum of the expected latent and previously generated observed discrepancies, adjoining a continuous node increases it to at most $(1+\hat L_f)e+d_i\|f_i-f'_i\|_\infty$; adjoining a categorical node increases it to at most $(1+(n_i-1)\hat L_f/2)e+n_i(n_i-1)\|f_i-f'_i\|_\infty/2$. Choose fixed constants $A\geqslant1$ and $B$ bounding these finitely many coefficients. Iterating $e_{k+1}\leqslant Ae_k+Bd(\theta,\theta')$ gives \[ e_k\leqslant A^ke_0+Bd(\theta,\theta')\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}A^r. \] Indeed, the formula holds for $k=0$, and multiplying its right side by $A$ and adding $Bd(\theta,\theta')$ gives the formula for $k+1$. Identical intervention values contribute zero discrepancy and remove their generation steps. Projection to the observed coordinates therefore proves \[ W(P^\theta(\boldsymbol V(\boldsymbol t)),P^{\theta'}(\boldsymbol V(\boldsymbol t)))\leqslant C d(\theta,\theta') \] uniformly over the intervention values, with $C$ depending on the fixed graph, dimensions, cardinalities and regularity bounds. The triangle inequality consequently makes $g(\theta)=W(P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol V),P^\theta(\boldsymbol V))$ Lipschitz in $d$; denote a Lipschitz constant by $C_g$. Now, we define $ \Theta _{n}$. Let  \begin{equation*} \mathcal{P}_{n} =\left\{{P}({\boldsymbol{U}}):\boldsymbol{U} \ \text{is the latent distribution of} \  \hat{\mathcal{M}} \in \text{NCM}_{\mathcal{G}} (\mathcal{F}_{0,n} ,\mathcal{F}_{1,n})\right\}. \end{equation*} Thus $\mathcal P_n$ consists of the latent population laws obtained by pushing forward the independent uniform and generator Gumbel inputs through the current positive-temperature generator networks. We denote $\Theta_n=\hat{\mathcal F}_{V_1,n}\times\cdots\times\hat{\mathcal F}_{V_{n_V},n}\times\mathcal P_n$, where \[ \hat{\mathcal F}_{V_i,n}=\begin{cases} \{f\in\mathcal F_{0,n}:\sup_x\|f(x)\|_1\leqslant K\},&V_i\text{ continuous},\\ \{q/\|q\|_1:q\in\mathcal F_{0,n},\ q(x)\in[0,\infty)^{n_i},\ \|q(x)\|_1>0\ \forall x,\ \operatorname{Lip}(q/\|q\|_1)\leqslant\hat L_f\},&V_i\text{ categorical}. \end{cases} \] The norms and Lipschitz bounds are evaluated on the structural input domains, and $\mathcal F_{0,n}$ is defined in \cref{thm:consistency}. Thus $\Theta_n\subset M$. Note that by construction, latent variables are independent and $ \mathcal{P}_{n}$ can be decomposed into direct produce $ \mathcal{P}_{n,1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{P}_{n,n_{U}}$. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be the set of restricted structural and generator network representations at sample size $n$, and let $\theta_\eta\in\Theta_n$ be the population parameter of a representation $\eta\in\mathcal A_n$. Let $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{m_n}$ be the common independent exogenous draws, including the categorical Gumbel coordinates, and write $H_\eta(\xi_l)$ for the resulting complete observed vector. Define \[ \Theta_\infty=\overline{\bigcup_n\Theta_n},\qquad P_{m_n}^\eta=\frac1{m_n}\sum_{l=1}^{m_n}\delta_{H_\eta(\xi_l)},\qquad h_n(\eta)=S_{\lambda_n}(P_n^{\theta^*},P_{m_n}^\eta), \] \[ f(\theta)=\mathbb E_{t\sim\mu_T}\mathbb E_{\mathcal M^\theta}[F(V_1(t),\ldots,V_{n_V}(t))]. \] The empirical constraint is a function of the representation $\eta$, whereas the population objective and $g(\theta)$ are functions of $\theta$. The optimization minimizes $f(\theta_\eta)$ over representations satisfying $h_n(\eta)\leqslant\alpha_n$.  For fixed $n$, pad the finitely many network architectures to their stated widths and encode each representation by its finitely many real weights and mixture probabilities. Finite products of Euclidean spaces and simplices are standard Borel spaces. Affine maps, ReLU, clipping and finite composition have jointly continuous evaluation in their weights and inputs. At the fixed temperature $\tau_n>0$, mixture weights can be written \[ \frac{p_j^{1/\tau_n}\exp(G_j/\tau_n)}{\sum_k p_k^{1/\tau_n}\exp(G_k/\tau_n)},\qquad p\in\Delta, \] whose denominator is positive even when some $p_j=0$; hence generator evaluation is jointly Borel.  The restrictions defining $\mathcal A_n$ are Borel restrictions on these parameters. To check this, choose a countable dense set in each continuous structural input domain. Continuity makes the output bound, coordinatewise nonnegativity and every Lipschitz inequality equivalent to their inequalities on that dense set or its Cartesian square. Each such inequality is Borel in the weights. For a nonnegative categorical raw network $q$, positivity on a compact input box $D_0$ is equivalent to membership in \[ \bigcup_{l=1}^\infty\bigcap_{x\in Q_0}\{\eta:\|q_\eta(x)\|_1\geqslant1/l\}, \] where $Q_0$ is countable and dense in $D_0$; continuity and attainment of a minimum prove both implications. Use the intersection of these conditions over a countable compact exhaustion when the full input domain is unbounded. On this Borel parameter set $q/\|q\|_1$ is jointly Borel and continuous in the input, so its Lipschitz restriction is again a countable family of Borel inequalities. The same dense-input tests apply to the raw Lipschitz restrictions before clipping. Thus $\mathcal A_n$ is standard Borel. These tests use dense input sets only.  The exogenous input space is a finite product of uniform cubes and real Gumbel coordinates, hence standard Borel. For a categorical propensity vector $p$, put $r_i=\exp(-g_i)/p_i$ when $p_i>0$ and $r_i=\infty$ when $p_i=0$. These extended-real functions are Borel. The smallest minimizing label is $i$ exactly when $r_i<r_j$ for every $j<i$ and $r_i\leqslant r_j$ for every $j>i$; this is a finite intersection of Borel comparisons. Induction through the finite topological order therefore proves joint Borel evaluation of $H_\eta(\xi)$ and of its interventional version $H_\eta(t,\xi)$. The function $F$ is bounded on the bounded observed range, so integration over the fixed exogenous law and $\mu_T$ makes $\eta\mapsto f(\theta_\eta)$ Borel. Finite empirical optimal transport and entropic transport values are continuous in their cost matrices: changing every cost by at most $a$ changes every transport objective, and hence its infimum, by at most $a$. Therefore the empirical Sinkhorn constraint $h_n(\eta)$ is jointly Borel in the representation and data. For every real $a$, the event $\{F_n<a\}$ is the projection of the Borel set defined by $h_n(\eta)\leqslant\alpha_n$ and $f(\theta_\eta)<a$, so it is analytic. The empirical optimal value and its limit events are measurable in the completed sample laws. If $L_F$ is a Lipschitz constant of $F$, the population coupling bound gives \[ |f(\theta)-f(\theta')|\leqslant L_F\mathbb E_{t\sim\mu_T}W(P^\theta(\boldsymbol V(t)),P^{\theta'}(\boldsymbol V(t)))\leqslant L_F C d(\theta,\theta'). \] Thus $f$ is continuous. We establish compactness, a sampling estimate for the current representations, and approximation of the true population parameter. \begin{enumerate}     \item Every continuous structural class has a common uniform output $1$-norm bound $K$ and Lipschitz constant $\hat L_f$ on a compact input domain. Every categorical structural class takes values in the compact simplex $\Delta_{n_i}$ and has the same common Lipschitz bound. Arzela--Ascoli makes each class relatively compact in the uniform norm. These classes are closed: for continuous maps a uniform limit satisfies $\|f(x)\|_1=\lim_r\|f_r(x)\|_1\leqslant K$ at every input $x$, uniform limits preserve the closed simplex constraint for categorical maps, and passing to the limit in $\|f_r(x)-f_r(y)\|_1\leqslant\hat L_f\|x-y\|_1$ preserves the Lipschitz constraint. Hence every $\mathcal F_{V_i}$ is compact. Probability measures on each compact latent cube form a compact space in the weak topology by Prokhorov's theorem. On a compact cube Wasserstein distance metrizes this topology. The finite product $M$ is consequently compact in $d$, and its closed subset $\Theta_\infty$ is compact.     \item We bound the complete observed simulation error, retaining paired observations and all categorical noise. Put $H_n=1+L_{1,n}+L_{2,n}$. The finite component counts of the specified separable architectures are fixed. For $0<\rho<1/2$, round the joint non-Gumbel latent vector to a grid of $1$-norm mesh at most $\rho$ in its $D_U$-dimensional cube. There are at most $C\rho^{-D_U}$ grid points. For each grid point and each possible categorical prefix in a topological order, evaluate the structural equations with that prefix fixed. Record the continuous outputs and categorical propensity vectors in a table, and round them within $\rho$, using a finite simplex grid for propensities. There are finitely many prefixes, independent of $n$. The tables have a finite set $\mathcal T_\rho$ of possible values with \[ \log|\mathcal T_\rho|\leqslant C\rho^{-D_U}\log(2+\rho^{-1}). \] Indeed, each entry lies in a fixed bounded finite-dimensional box, so a grid has at most $(C/\rho)^C$ choices, and the number of entries is at most $C\rho^{-D_U}$. With a categorical prefix fixed, induction through the continuous structural equations bounds their change under a latent perturbation of size $\rho$ by $C\rho$: each new difference is at most $\hat L_f$ times the sum of previous and latent differences. The categorical propensities have the same bound. Thus, as long as the selected categorical prefixes agree, the original and table outputs differ by at most $C\rho$, and the corresponding propensities differ coordinatewise by at most $a=C\rho$.  The table simulation uses the original categorical Gumbel draws. Write $E_k=\exp(-g_k)$; these are independent unit-rate exponential variables, and a propensity vector $p$ selects $\arg\min_k E_k/p_k$, with $E_k/0=\infty$. For a table propensity vector $q\in\Delta_N$, call label $i$ robust if $q_i>a$ and \[ \frac{E_i}{q_i-a}<\min_{j\ne i}\frac{E_j}{q_j+a}. \] A robust label wins for every propensity vector whose coordinates differ from $q$ by at most $a$. The robust-label events are disjoint. For $q_i>a$, integrating the density of $E_i$ and the survival probabilities of the other exponentials gives \[ \mathbb P(i\text{ robust})=\int_0^\infty\exp\left(-s\left(1+\frac{\sum_{j\ne i}(q_j+a)}{q_i-a}\right)\right)\,ds =\frac{q_i-a}{q_i-a+\sum_{j\ne i}(q_j+a)}. \] For $q_i\leqslant a$ this probability is zero. Consequently, \[ \mathbb P(i\text{ robust})\geqslant\frac{(q_i-a)_+}{1+Na}. \] Summing and using $\sum_i(q_i-a)_+\geqslant1-Na$ bounds the probability of no robust label by $2Na/(1+Na)$ when $Na<1$, and the trivial bound $1\leqslant2Na$ covers $Na\geqslant1$. For each table and generator representation let $b$ be the indicator that a nonrobust choice occurs at any table prefix. Independence of the categorical noise from the generated latent vector and a union bound over the finitely many prefixes give $\mathbb E b\leqslant C\rho$. If $b=0$, induction over the categorical nodes forces the original and table prefixes to agree. Consequently, writing $\widetilde H$ for the table observed map and $B_V$ for a common bound on the observed $1$-norm diameter, \[ \|H_\eta(\xi)-\widetilde H(\xi)\|_1\leqslant C\rho+B_V b(\xi). \] This is a pointwise bound, including zero propensities.  We bound the complexity of finite-type indicators and ambiguity indicators. A table simulation has type $(u,c)$, where $u$ is its latent grid index and $c$ its complete categorical label vector; its observed output is a fixed vector for each type. There are at most $J=C\rho^{-D_U}$ types. Include the indicators of membership in every subset of these types, and the ambiguity indicators $b$, in a scalar class $\mathcal B_{n,\rho}$.  Here is an explicit standard Borel parameterization of this entire indicator class. Let $\Gamma_n$ be the finite-dimensional generator weight space with its mixture simplex factors, and let generator parameters range over all of $\Gamma_n$. This supplies an envelope for every restricted generator used in the optimization. A parameter consists of $\gamma\in\Gamma_n$, a table in the finite set $\mathcal T_\rho$, and a finite tag specifying either a subset of the at most $J$ types or the ambiguity indicator. This is a finite union of products of standard Borel spaces. Generator evaluation is jointly Borel by the positive-denominator mixture formula. Round its clipped latent output using fixed half-open grid cells, with the last cell closed at the endpoint; the grid index is a finite-valued Borel function. For each fixed table and grid index, the table simulation uses finitely many categorical race comparisons. In the notation $r_i=\exp(-g_i)/q_i$, with $r_i=\infty$ at $q_i=0$, the smallest-label rule is the finite system $r_i<r_j$ for $j<i$ and $r_i\leqslant r_j$ for $j>i$, so its selected label is Borel. The robust-label events are Borel too: when $q_i>a$ all their denominators are positive, and when $q_i\leqslant a$ the event is empty. Their finite unions and complements make $b$ jointly Borel. Type-subset membership is a finite union of these Borel events. Thus $\mathcal B_{n,\rho}$ has jointly Borel evaluation on a standard Borel parameter space, including zero propensities, grid boundaries and all ties. When using the ambient Euclidean input space in Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein}, clip the uniform input coordinates to their cubes; this changes no sample value and preserves joint Borel evaluation. The parameter envelope has precisely the same architecture and finite tags as those counted in the growth bound. For each continuous scalar dual test $h$, its normalized square-root transform is jointly Borel by composition. Consequently the structural condition of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} holds for these families, without approximation of selector parameters.  On $M_0$ fixed exogenous inputs, the latent grid indices are determined by at most $C M_0/\rho$ scalar generator comparisons. The ReLU blocks have $P\leqslant C H_n$ parameters and at most $C H_n$ layers. Within a fixed activation pattern, their outputs are polynomials in the parameters of degree at most $C H_n$. For a positive-temperature mixture write its weights as $a_j R_j/\sum_k a_kR_k$, where $a_j=p_j^{1/\tau_n}\geqslant0$, $\sum_j a_j>0$, and $R_j=\exp(G_j/\tau_n)$ is fixed on each input. Treat the $a_j$ as additional free parameters. Clearing the positive denominator in a grid comparison leaves a polynomial of degree at most $C H_n+1$. Truncation adds only fixed-degree comparisons. The polynomial sign bound in Lemma 17 of \cite{bartlett2019nearly}, applied successively to the activation comparisons in each layer and then to these grid comparisons, gives at most \[ (C(M_0+H_n)H_n/\rho)^{C H_n^2} \] latent grid patterns: at each layer the sign bound contributes at most $(C(M_0+H_n)H_n/\rho)^{C P}$, and there are at most $C H_n$ layers. For a fixed table and grid pattern, the categorical race comparisons and every table output on these inputs are determined. The subgraph growth of $\mathcal B_{n,\rho}$ is therefore at most this number times $|\mathcal T_\rho|2^J$: a subset of the types has $2^J$ choices, and an ambiguity indicator needs no additional choices. ### `prop:lip-ate` (`Main.tex:309-317`)

- as printed: \label{prop:Lip_ATE} Given two causal models $ \mathcal{M} ,\hat{\mathcal{M}} \in\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F}_L,\boldsymbol{U})$ satisfying \cref{assump:independence_u} and \cref{assump:Lip_and_bounded}, let their observational distributions be $ \nu ,\mu $. Suppose the norms of all variables are bounded by $K>0$. If (1) (Overlap) $ \nu $ is absolutely continuous with respect to one probability measure $P$ and the density $ p_{\nu }\left( t|\text{Pa}( T) =x\right) \geqslant \delta >0 $ for x almost surely and $ t\in [ t_{1} ,t_{2}]$ and (2) (No Confounding) there is no hidden confounder in the causal graph $\mathcal{G}$, we have \begin{equation*} \begin{aligned} \int _{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}[ Y( t)] -\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}} }[\hat{Y}( t)])^{2} P(dt) & \leqslant \frac{2C_{W}}{\delta } W( \mu ,\nu ) +2(L+1)^{n_{V}} W^{2}( \mu ,\nu )( t_{2} -t_{1}) , \end{aligned} \end{equation*} where $ C_{W} =4(L+1)^{n_{V}} K+2K\max\left\{(L+1)^{n_{V}} ,1\right\}$.

For any coupling of the observational laws, the absolute difference of the outcome means is at most the expected absolute difference of the outcome coordinates, which is at most the expected $1$-norm distance of the observed vectors. Now, suppose that $Y$ is a descendant of $T$. Let $X=\text{Pa}(T)$, and let $A$ be the vector of all observed nodes other than $T$ that are not descendants of $T$. In particular, $X$ is a subvector of $A$. Every observed parent of a node in $A$ also belongs to $A$: a parent equal to $T$, or descended from $T$, would make that node a descendant of $T$. By the canonical representation and the absence of hidden confounding, the noises belonging to distinct observed nodes are independent. Thus $A$ is generated without the noise of $T$ or any descendant of $T$, and the descendant noises are independent of $(A,T)$. Conditional on $A=a$, the equation of $T$ uses only $X=x$ and its own independent noise. Consequently, \[ \nu(dt|A=a)=\nu(dt|X=x). \] For each $\mathcal{N}\in\{\mathcal{M},\hat{\mathcal{M}}\}$, fix $A=a$ and $T=t$ and generate the descendants of $T$ in topological order using their independent noises with their laws in $\mathcal{N}$. Denote the resulting mean of the outcome by $g_{\mathcal{N}}(a,t)$. These means are finite: categorical outputs have finite ranges, and the Lipschitz bound for a continuous structural function bounds its output by its value at a fixed input plus $L$ times the input distance; induction through the finite graph, using bounded non-Gumbel noises, gives finite first moments at every fixed $(a,t)$. Independence of the descendant noises from $(A,T)$ shows that $g_{\mathcal{N}}$ is a version of the observational outcome regression given $(A,T)$. The intervention leaves the equations generating $A$ unchanged, so its distribution is its observational marginal. Therefore, \[ \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}[Y(t)]=\int g_{\mathcal{M}}(a,t)\nu_A(da),\qquad \mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}[\hat{Y}(t)]=\int g_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}(a,t)\mu_A(da), \] where $\nu_A$ and $\mu_A$ are the observational marginals of $A$. For a continuous descendant $V_i$, couple its outputs at two parent histories $h,h'$ using the same private noise. The structural Lipschitz bound gives \[ \mathbb{E}\|V_i(h)-V_i(h')\|\leqslant L\|h-h'\|. \] For a categorical descendant, let $\pi_i(h)$ be its propensity vector after integrating its private non-Gumbel noise. The canonical Gumbel rule has categorical probabilities equal to this vector. Integration of the propensity Lipschitz bound gives \[ \|\pi_i(h)-\pi_i(h')\|\leqslant L\|h-h'\|. \] Place mass $\min\{\pi_{i,j}(h),\pi_{i,j}(h')\}$ on each equal pair $(j,j)$. The remaining masses in the two marginals have the same total mass and disjoint supports; coupling these remaining masses gives disagreement probability \[ 1-\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}\min\{\pi_{i,j}(h),\pi_{i,j}(h')\} =\frac12\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}|\pi_{i,j}(h)-\pi_{i,j}(h')|. \] Two labels in $[n_i]$ differ by at most $n_i-1$, so this coupling satisfies \[ \mathbb{E}|V_i(h)-V_i(h')|\leqslant\frac{n_i-1}{2}\|\pi_i(h)-\pi_i(h')\|\leqslant LD\|h-h'\|. \] The continuous bound is also at most $LD\|h-h'\|$, since $D\geqslant1$.  Starting at fixed inputs $(a,t)$ and $(a',t')$, use these couplings successively for the descendants, conditional on the accumulated histories. Let $E_r$ be the expected $1$-norm distance between these histories after $r$ descendants have been generated. Projection onto a parent history cannot increase this distance. Hence \[ E_0=\|a-a'\|+|t-t'|,\qquad E_{r+1}\leqslant E_r+LD E_r=(1+LD)E_r. \] Induction gives $E_r\leqslant(1+LD)^rE_0$: the assertion holds at $r=0$, and the recurrence multiplies its bound by $1+LD$ at the next step. There are at most $n_V$ descendants. Projection onto the outcome coordinate, followed by $|\mathbb{E}Y-\mathbb{E}Y'|\leqslant\mathbb{E}|Y-Y'|$, therefore gives \[ |g_{\mathcal{N}}(a,t)-g_{\mathcal{N}}(a',t')|\leqslant L_y(\|a-a'\|+|t-t'|). \] This argument applies to each of the two models without conditioning on latent inputs shared with observed ancestors.  Let $Q$ be the set of allowed inputs $s=(a,t)$ whose numerical coordinates all lie in $[-K,K]$. Categorical coordinates retain their categorical ranges. The numerical dimension of $(A,T)$ is at most $q$, so any $s,s'\in Q$ satisfy $\|s-s'\|\leqslant2Kq$. Both observational laws of $(A,T)$ give $Q$ probability one. For each $\mathcal{N}\in\{\mathcal{M},\hat{\mathcal{M}}\}$, the observational outcome bound and the conditional expectation identity give $|g_{\mathcal{N}}(A,T)|\leqslant K$ almost surely under its own observational law. Choose an input $s_{\mathcal{N}}\in Q$ where this inequality holds. For every $s\in Q$, the Lipschitz inequality then yields \[ |g_{\mathcal{N}}(s)|\leqslant|g_{\mathcal{N}}(s_{\mathcal{N}})|+L_y\|s-s_{\mathcal{N}}\|\leqslant K+2KqL_y=B. \] Thus the structural regression versions are bounded by $B$ on $Q$, including inputs outside their observational supports. Put $f_y(a,t)=g_{\mathcal{M}}(a,t)$. Recall that $ \nu,\mu $ are the observation distributions of $\mathcal{M}$ and $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ respectively in \cref{prop:Lip_ATE}.  Put $\hat f_y(a,t)=g_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}(a,t)$. Its construction gives a version of $\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}[\hat Y|A=a,T=t]$, the $L_y$-Lipschitz inequality, the interventional identity, and the bound $|\hat f_y(a,t)|\leqslant B$ for $(a,t)\in Q$.  We use the test-function argument of Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lip_condition} on the vector covariate $s=(a,t)$, with regression bound $B$, and give the calculation explicitly. Write \[ d(s)=\hat f_y(s)-f_y(s),\qquad G(s,y)=d(s)y,\qquad h(s)=d(s)\hat f_y(s). \] On $Q$, the established bounds imply $|d(s)|\leqslant2B$ and $|d(s)-d(s')|\leqslant2L_y\|s-s'\|$. For $s,s'\in Q$ and $|y|,|y'|\leqslant K\leqslant B$, \begin{align*} |G(s,y)-G(s',y')| &\leqslant2B|y-y'|+2KL_y\|s-s'\|\\ &\leqslant2B\max\{L_y,1\}(\|s-s'\|+|y-y'|),\\ |h(s)-h(s')| &\leqslant |d(s)|\,|\hat f_y(s)-\hat f_y(s')|+|\hat f_y(s')|\,|d(s)-d(s')|\\ &\leqslant4BL_y\|s-s'\|. \end{align*} Conditioning on the covariate gives $\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[G]=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[G]=\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[df_y]$. Since $h-df_y=d^2$, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}_{\nu}[d(A,T)^2] &=(\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[G]-\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[G])+(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[h]-\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[h])\\ &\leqslant\bigl(2B\max\{L_y,1\}+4BL_y\bigr)W(\mu,\nu) =C_WW(\mu,\nu). \end{align*} For each Wasserstein bound, integrate the corresponding displayed Lipschitz inequality against any coupling of the observational laws and take the infimum of its expected $1$-norm cost. Both endpoints belong to the domains on which these inequalities were proved. Projection onto $(A,T,Y)$ or $(A,T)$ cannot increase that cost.  Set $I=[t_1,t_2]$. Observational boundedness gives $\nu_T(\mathbb{R}\setminus[-K,K])=0$. The conditional treatment law given $A$ equals the law given $X=\text{Pa}(T)$. Integrating the overlap bound therefore gives \[ 0=\nu_T(I\setminus[-K,K])\geqslant\delta P(I\setminus[-K,K]), \] so $P(I\setminus[-K,K])=0$. Thus, for $P$-almost every $t\in I$ and for either observational marginal of $A$, the input $(A,t)$ belongs to $Q$. The overlap assumption now yields \begin{align*} C_WW(\mu,\nu) &\geqslant\int (f_y(a,t)-\hat f_y(a,t))^2\nu(dt|A=a)\nu_A(da)\\ &\geqslant\delta\int_I\int(f_y(a,t)-\hat f_y(a,t))^2\nu_A(da)P(dt)\\ &\geqslant\delta\int_I b(t)^2P(dt), \end{align*} where $b(t)=\int(f_y(a,t)-\hat f_y(a,t))\nu_A(da)$. The last inequality is Jensen's inequality for the probability measure $\nu_A$. Put \[ c(t)=\int\hat f_y(a,t)\nu_A(da)-\int\hat f_y(a,t)\mu_A(da). \] For $P$-almost every $t\in I$, integrate the Lipschitz bound of $\hat f_y$ in $a$ against a coupling of the two marginals and take the infimum to obtain $|c(t)|\leqslant L_yW(\nu_A,\mu_A)\leqslant L_yW(\mu,\nu)$. The interventional identities give \[ \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}[Y(t)]-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}[\hat Y(t)]=b(t)+c(t). \] Since $2b(t)c(t)\leqslant b(t)^2+c(t)^2$, it follows, for $P$-almost every $t\in I$, that \[ (\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}[Y(t)]-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}[\hat Y(t)])^2 \leqslant2b(t)^2+2L_y^2W^2(\mu,\nu). \] Integrating this inequality against $P(dt)$ on $[t_1,t_2]$ and using the bound on the integral of $b(t)^2$ gives \begin{align*} \int_{t_1}^{t_2}(\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{M}}[Y(t)]-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{\mathcal{M}}}[\hat Y(t)])^2P(dt) &\leqslant2\int_{t_1}^{t_2}b(t)^2P(dt)+2L_y^2W^2(\mu,\nu)\int_{t_1}^{t_2}1\,P(dt)\\ &\leqslant\frac{2C_W}{\delta}W(\mu,\nu)+2L_y^2W^2(\mu,\nu)P([t_1,t_2]). \end{align*}
- why: (a) The statement is false for mixed variables: Lipschitz categorical propensities do not make the categorical generation map Lipschitz, and category labels can amplify the outcome regression beyond $(L+1)^{n_V}$. (b) Independently, even with continuous variables, conditioning on $X=\text{Pa}(T)$ need not leave the latent inputs needed for $Y$ independent of $X$; an observed ancestor can enter both $X$ and $Y$, invalidating the asserted composition argument and regression bound. (c) The proof derives a quadratic coefficient $2L_y^2$, but the statement replaces it by $2(L+1)^{n_V}$; the stated bound on $L_y$ does not justify this substitution. (d) Integrating the constant remainder against $P(dt)$ produces $P([t_1,t_2])$, not $t_2-t_1$; the nondescendant branch likewise switches to $dt$. Dismiss the wiring lint: the regression and boundedness conditions of Lemma~\ref{lemma:Lip_condition} are conditions this proof attempts to derive, rather than additional standing hypotheses. The failed regression derivation is a correctness defect.

### `thm:rate` (`Main.tex:319-321`)

- as printed: \label{cor:rate} Let $F, \mu_T$ in \cref{thm:consistency} to be $ F(\boldsymbol{V}) = Y, \mu_T \sim \text{Unif}([t_1, t_2]), \epsilon >0 $. Suppose that the assumptions in Proposition \ref{prop:Lip_ATE} and \cref{thm:consistency} hold, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-2})$, we have $ | F_n - F_*| \leqslant O(\sqrt{\alpha_n})$, where $F_n,F_*,\alpha_n$ are defined in \cref{thm:consistency}.
- corrected: Let $F,\mu_T$ in \cref{thm:consistency} be $F(\boldsymbol V)=Y$, $\mu_T\sim\operatorname{Unif}([t_1,t_2])$, and $\epsilon>0$. Suppose that $t_1<t_2$. Suppose that the assumptions in Proposition \ref{prop:Lip_ATE} and \cref{thm:consistency} hold. Suppose in addition that $\mu_T\ll P$ and \[ A_T^2=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(\frac{d\mu_T}{dP}(t)\right)^2P(dt)<\infty, \] where $P$ is the reference probability measure in Proposition~\ref{prop:Lip_ATE}. Use the network classes $\mathcal F_{0,n}$ and $\mathcal F_{1,n}$ and the population structural classes specified in \cref{thm:consistency}. In (\ref{eq:opt_empiri}), restrict each continuous structural network $\hat f_i\in\mathcal F_{0,n}$ to satisfy $\sup_x\|\hat f_i(x)\|_1\leqslant K$ on its full structural input domain, and restrict each categorical raw structural network $q\in\mathcal F_{0,n}$ to satisfy $q(x)\in[0,\infty)^{n_i}$, $\|q(x)\|_1>0$ for every structural input $x$, and \[ \operatorname{Lip}\left(x\mapsto\frac{q(x)}{\|q(x)\|_1}\right)\leqslant\hat L_f. \] For each sample size, obtain every candidate empirical law by evaluating the candidate on the same $m_n$ independent draws of its uniform and Gumbel exogenous inputs, independent of the observational sample. Let $F_n$ be the optimal value of this restricted optimization, retaining the objective and Sinkhorn constraint of (\ref{eq:opt_empiri}). Put \[ D_U=\sum_{j=1}^{n_U}d_j^U,\qquad D=\max\{1,D_U\}, \] where the sum includes only the non-Gumbel latent variables. Take $\alpha_n=\epsilon_n+s_n$, with positive tolerances chosen as sufficiently large constant multiples of the respective quantities in \[ \epsilon_n=O\left(W_{0,n}^{-1/d_{\max}^{\text{in}}}+\sum_{i=1}^2L_{i,n}^{-2/d_{\max}^U}+\tau_n(1-\log\tau_n)\right), \] \[ s_n=O\left(m_n^{-1/(D+2)}\log m_n+\frac{(L_{1,n}+L_{2,n})\log m_n}{\sqrt{m_n}}+n^{-1/\max\{2,D_U\}}\log^2n+\log(nm_n)\lambda_n\right). \] Then, with probability at least $1-O(n^{-2})$, we have $|F_n-F_*|\leqslant O(\sqrt{\alpha_n})$, where $F_*$ is defined in \cref{thm:consistency} and $F_n,\alpha_n$ are specified here.

- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] We establish feasibility and the complete-observation sampling bounds for the specified restricted optimization. Write $\eta$ for a network representation, $\theta_\eta$ for its population SCM parameter, and $\theta^*$ for the true parameter. For two population parameters define \[ d(\theta,\theta')=\sum_{i=1}^{n_V}\|f_i-f'_i\|_\infty+\sum_{j=1}^{n_U}W(P(U_j),P(U'_j)), \] using normalized categorical propensity functions in the first sum. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be the set of admissible representations. With common independent exogenous draws $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{m_n}$, let $H_\eta(\xi_l)$ be the complete observed vector and put \[ P_{m_n}^\eta=\frac1{m_n}\sum_{l=1}^{m_n}\delta_{H_\eta(\xi_l)},\qquad h_n(\eta)=S_{\lambda_n}(P_n^{\theta^*},P_{m_n}^\eta),\qquad g(\theta)=W(P^{\theta^*},P^\theta). \] All distributions in these expressions are distributions of the complete observed vector. Write $f(\theta)=\mathbb E_{t\sim\mu_T}\mathbb E_{\mathcal M^\theta}[F(\boldsymbol V(t))]$ for the objective.  For fixed $n$, pad the finitely many network architectures to their stated widths and encode each representation by its finitely many real weights and mixture probabilities. Finite products of Euclidean spaces and simplices are standard Borel spaces. Affine maps, ReLU, clipping and finite composition have jointly continuous evaluation in their weights and inputs. At the fixed temperature $\tau_n>0$, mixture weights can be written \[ \frac{p_j^{1/\tau_n}\exp(G_j/\tau_n)}{\sum_k p_k^{1/\tau_n}\exp(G_k/\tau_n)},\qquad p\in\Delta, \] whose denominator is positive even when some $p_j=0$; hence generator evaluation is jointly Borel.  The restrictions defining $\mathcal A_n$ are Borel restrictions on these parameters. Choose a countable dense set in each continuous structural input domain. Continuity makes the output bound, coordinatewise nonnegativity and every Lipschitz inequality equivalent to their inequalities on that dense set or its Cartesian square, and each such inequality is Borel in the weights. For a nonnegative categorical raw network $q$, positivity on a compact input box $D_0$ is equivalent to membership in \[ \bigcup_{l=1}^\infty\bigcap_{x\in Q_0}\{\eta:\|q_\eta(x)\|_1\geqslant1/l\}, \] where $Q_0$ is countable and dense in $D_0$. Positivity implies a positive minimum on the compact box; conversely the dense-set lower bound extends by continuity. Intersect these conditions over a countable compact exhaustion if the full domain is unbounded. On the resulting Borel parameter set $q/\|q\|_1$ is jointly Borel and continuous in the input, so its Lipschitz restriction is another countable family of Borel inequalities. The raw Lipschitz restrictions before clipping have the same dense-input characterization. Thus $\mathcal A_n$ is standard Borel.  The exogenous space is a finite product of uniform cubes and real Gumbel coordinates. For categorical propensities $p$, define $r_i=\exp(-g_i)/p_i$ for $p_i>0$ and $r_i=\infty$ for $p_i=0$. The smallest minimizing label is $i$ precisely when $r_i<r_j$ for all $j<i$ and $r_i\leqslant r_j$ for all $j>i$. These are Borel comparisons of extended-real Borel functions. Induction in topological order proves that both $H_\eta(\xi)$ and $H_\eta(t,\xi)$ are jointly Borel. Integration of the bounded objective on the observed range makes $f(\theta_\eta)$ Borel in $\eta$: parameter integrals of bounded Borel functions are Borel by the monotone class theorem. Empirical transport values are continuous in the cost matrix, since a uniform change of at most $a$ in costs changes every coupling objective and its infimum by at most $a$. Hence $h_n$ is jointly Borel in parameters and data. The event $\{F_n<a\}$ is the projection of the Borel set $\{(\eta,\text{data}):h_n(\eta)\leqslant\alpha_n,\ f(\theta_\eta)<a\}$, so is analytic and measurable in the completed sample law.  First derive population continuity in the fixed dimensions. Couple corresponding independent non-Gumbel latent laws optimally and take the product of their couplings. The expected joint latent $1$-norm discrepancy is the sum of their marginal Wasserstein distances. Generate the observed nodes in topological order. At a continuous node, the expected new discrepancy is at most $d_i\|f_i-f'_i\|_\infty+\hat L_f$ times the expected input discrepancy. At a categorical node, place mass $\min\{p_k,p'_k\}$ on each equal label pair and couple the remaining disjoint residual masses. Its disagreement probability is $\|p-p'\|_1/2$, so its expected label discrepancy is at most $(n_i-1)\|p-p'\|_1/2$. The normalized Lipschitz restrictions bound this by \[ \frac{n_i(n_i-1)}2\|f_i-f'_i\|_\infty+\frac{(n_i-1)\hat L_f}2\mathbb E\|\text{input}-\text{input}'\|. \] Choose fixed $A\geqslant1$ and $B$ bounding these finitely many coefficients. If $e_k$ is the expected discrepancy of the latent vector and generated history, then $e_0\leqslant d(\theta,\theta')$ and $e_{k+1}\leqslant Ae_k+Bd(\theta,\theta')$. Induction gives \[ e_k\leqslant A^ke_0+Bd(\theta,\theta')\sum_{r=0}^{k-1}A^r: \] the assertion is equality at $k=0$, and multiplying its right-hand side by $A$ and adding $Bd(\theta,\theta')$ gives the asserted expression at $k+1$. Projection onto the observed vector yields $W(P^\theta,P^{\theta'})\leqslant C d(\theta,\theta')$. Identical intervention values contribute zero discrepancy and remove their generation steps, giving the same bound for every intervention. The triangle inequality consequently makes $g$ Lipschitz; denote a Lipschitz constant by $C_g$.  We now bound the complete observed simulation error, retaining paired observations and all categorical noise. Put $H_n=1+L_{1,n}+L_{2,n}$. The component counts of the specified separable architectures are fixed. For $0<\rho<1/2$, round the joint non-Gumbel latent vector to a grid of $1$-norm mesh at most $\rho$ in its $D_U$-dimensional cube. There are at most $C\rho^{-D_U}$ grid points. For each grid point and each possible categorical prefix in a topological order, evaluate the structural equations with that prefix fixed. Record the continuous outputs and categorical propensity vectors in a table, and round them within $\rho$, using a finite simplex grid for propensities. There are finitely many prefixes, independent of $n$. The tables have a finite set $\mathcal T_\rho$ of possible values with \[ \log|\mathcal T_\rho|\leqslant C\rho^{-D_U}\log(2+\rho^{-1}). \] Indeed, each entry lies in a fixed bounded finite-dimensional box, so a grid has at most $(C/\rho)^C$ choices, and there are at most $C\rho^{-D_U}$ entries. With a categorical prefix fixed, induction through the continuous structural equations bounds their change under a latent perturbation of size $\rho$ by $C\rho$: each new difference is at most $\hat L_f$ times the sum of previous and latent differences. Categorical propensities satisfy the same bound. Thus, while the selected categorical prefixes agree, the original and table outputs differ by at most $C\rho$, and corresponding propensities differ coordinatewise by at most $a=C\rho$.  The table simulation uses the original categorical Gumbel draws. Write $E_k=\exp(-g_k)$; these are independent unit-rate exponential variables, and a propensity vector $p$ selects $\arg\min_k E_k/p_k$, with $E_k/0=\infty$. For a table propensity vector $q\in\Delta_N$, call label $i$ robust if $q_i>a$ and \[ \frac{E_i}{q_i-a}<\min_{j\ne i}\frac{E_j}{q_j+a}. \] A robust label wins for every propensity vector whose coordinates differ from $q$ by at most $a$. The robust-label events are disjoint. When $q_i>a$, integration of the independent exponential densities gives \[ \mathbb P(i\text{ robust})=\frac{q_i-a}{q_i-a+\sum_{j\ne i}(q_j+a)}. \] When $q_i\leqslant a$, the probability is zero. In either case it is at least $(q_i-a)_+/(1+Na)$. Summing and using $\sum_i(q_i-a)_+\geqslant1-Na$ bounds the probability of no robust label by $2Na/(1+Na)$ when $Na<1$; when $Na\geqslant1$, the bound $1\leqslant2Na$ suffices. For each table and generator representation let $b$ indicate that a nonrobust choice occurs at any table prefix. Independence of categorical noise from the generated latent vector and a union bound over the finitely many prefixes give $\mathbb E b\leqslant C\rho$. If $b=0$, induction over the categorical nodes forces the original and table prefixes to agree. Thus, with $\widetilde H$ the table observed map and $B_V$ a common observed $1$-norm diameter bound, \[ \|H_\eta(\xi)-\widetilde H(\xi)\|\leqslant C\rho+B_V b(\xi). \] This bound includes zero propensities.  A table simulation has type $(u,c)$, where $u$ is its latent grid index and $c$ its complete categorical label vector; its observed output is fixed for each type. There are at most $J=C\rho^{-D_U}$ types. Include the indicators of membership in every subset of these types, and the ambiguity indicators $b$, in a scalar class $\mathcal B_{n,\rho}$.  To verify the structural condition of Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} for this class, let $\Gamma_n$ be the entire finite-dimensional generator weight space with its mixture simplex factors. This gives a measurable envelope for the restricted generator representations. Index indicators by a parameter in $\Gamma_n$, a table in the finite set $\mathcal T_\rho$, and a finite tag specifying either a subset of the at most $J$ types or the ambiguity indicator. This is a standard Borel space. Generator evaluation is jointly Borel by the positive-denominator mixture formula. Its clipped output has a Borel grid index when cells are half-open and the final cell includes its endpoint. Given the table and grid index, each categorical choice is a finite Borel comparison using $r_i<r_j$ for $j<i$ and $r_i\leqslant r_j$ for $j>i$, with $r_i=\infty$ for zero table propensity. Each robust event is a Borel comparison with positive denominators on $q_i>a$, and is empty on $q_i\leqslant a$. Finite unions and complements therefore give jointly Borel ambiguity and type-subset indicators. This includes all ties, grid boundaries and zero propensities. Clip uniform exogenous coordinates outside their cubes to view these functions on the ambient Euclidean input space; the values on the sampled inputs do not change. Composing a jointly Borel indicator with a continuous scalar dual function and its normalized square-root transform preserves joint Borel evaluation. Thus all the classes to which the lemma's concentration argument is applied have the required standard Borel parameterization. The envelope uses the same architectural parameters and finite tags as the growth calculation; no density assertion for discontinuous selectors is needed.  On $M_0$ fixed exogenous inputs, the latent grid indices are determined by at most $CM_0/\rho$ scalar generator comparisons. The ReLU blocks have at most $CH_n$ parameters and $CH_n$ layers. Within a fixed activation pattern their outputs are polynomials in the parameters of degree at most $CH_n$. For a positive-temperature mixture write its weights as $a_jR_j/\sum_k a_kR_k$, where $a_j=p_j^{1/\tau_n}\geqslant0$, $\sum_j a_j>0$, and $R_j=\exp(G_j/\tau_n)$ is fixed on each input. Treat the $a_j$ as additional free parameters. Clearing the positive denominator in a grid comparison leaves a polynomial of degree at most $CH_n+1$. Truncation adds fixed-degree comparisons. The polynomial sign bound in Lemma 17 of \cite{bartlett2019nearly}, applied successively to activation comparisons in each layer and then to grid comparisons, gives at most \[ (C(M_0+H_n)H_n/\rho)^{CH_n^2} \] latent grid patterns: each layer contributes at most $(C(M_0+H_n)H_n/\rho)^{CH_n}$, and there are at most $CH_n$ layers. For a fixed table and grid pattern all categorical race comparisons and table outputs on these inputs are determined. The growth of $\mathcal B_{n,\rho}$ is therefore at most this number times $|\mathcal T_\rho|2^J$. Hence its pseudo-dimension satisfies \[ v_n(\rho)\leqslant C\left(\rho^{-D_U}\log(2+\rho^{-1})+H_n^2\log(2+H_n/\rho)\right). \] To obtain this bound explicitly, put $A_0=\log|\mathcal T_\rho|+J\log2$ and $B_0=CH_n^2$ in the shattering inequality \[ M_0\log2\leqslant A_0+B_0\log(C(M_0+H_n)H_n/\rho). \] If $M_0\leqslant4A_0/\log2$, the first term suffices. Otherwise the inequality bounds $M_0$ by $CB_0\log(2+B_0H_n/\rho)+CB_0\log(2+A_0/B_0)$; the established bound on $A_0$ gives the displayed estimate.  Put \[ r_n=m_n^{-1/(D+2)}\log m_n+H_nm_n^{-1/2}\log m_n. \] The depth schedule in \cref{thm:consistency} gives $H_n=O(m_n^{d_{\max}^U/(2d_{\max}^U+4)})$, so $r_n\rightarrow0$. For sufficiently large $n$ take $\rho=r_n$ and apply Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} to $\mathcal B_{n,r_n}$ with scalar output. These functions take values in $\{0,1\}$, and the Wasserstein distance of their Bernoulli output laws equals the absolute difference of their means. With tolerances $\delta=r_n$ and $\epsilon=Cr_n$, its failure exponent is bounded above by \[ C_1\left((1+r_n^{-1})\log(2+r_n^{-1})+r_n^{-D_U}\log^2(2+r_n^{-1})+H_n^2\log(2+H_n/r_n)\log(2+r_n^{-1})\right)-cC^2m_nr_n^2. \] Here $\log(2+H_n/r_n)=O(\log m_n)$ and \[ m_nr_n^2\geqslant m_n^{D/(D+2)}\log^2m_n+H_n^2\log^2m_n, \] whereas $r_n^{-D_U}\leqslant m_n^{D_U/(D+2)}(\log m_n)^{-D_U}$ and $r_n^{-1}\leqslant m_n^{1/(D+2)}/\log m_n$. Since $D\geqslant\max\{D_U,1\}$, a sufficiently large fixed $C$ makes the failure probability $O(m_n^{-3})$. On the complementary event every type-subset probability and ambiguity-indicator mean differs from its empirical counterpart by at most $Cr_n$. The type-subset bound controls total variation between population and empirical type laws. Couple common type masses identically and residual masses arbitrarily; their table-output Wasserstein distance is at most $B_VCr_n$. Coupling original and table outputs on the same draw bounds their population discrepancy by $C\rho+B_V\mathbb E b$ and their empirical discrepancy by $C\rho+B_Vm_n^{-1}\sum_l b(\xi_l)$. Both are at most $Cr_n$ by the ambiguity estimate. The triangle inequality therefore gives \[ \sup_{\eta\in\mathcal A_n}W(P^{\theta_\eta},P_{m_n}^\eta)\leqslant Cr_n \] with probability at least $1-O(m_n^{-3})$.  For the observational sample let $C$ be its complete categorical label vector, taking values in a fixed finite set. Conditional on $C=c$, all continuous observations equal a deterministic map $\Phi_c(U_1,\ldots,U_{n_U})$, obtained by fixing the categorical labels and evaluating the continuous equations in topological order. Their Lipschitz bounds make $\Phi_c$ Lipschitz with a constant uniform over these finitely many labels. The conditional joint latent laws $\mu_c=P((U_1,\ldots,U_{n_U})\mid C=c)$ are supported on the bounded $D_U$-dimensional cube and need not be products. Write $p_c=P(C=c)$ and $N_c$ for sample counts. If $p_c=0$, then $N_c=0$ almost surely. For $p_c>0$, binomial concentration gives $N_c\geqslant np_c/2$ except on an exponentially small event. Conditional on the sample labels, latents in category $c$ are independent with law $\mu_c$.  For $D_U\geqslant1$, Theorem 2 of \cite{fournier2015rate} applied to these conditional joint latent laws bounds their empirical Wasserstein errors by $C_cn^{-1/\max\{2,D_U\}}\log^2n$ with failure probability $O(n^{-4})$, uniformly for $np_c/2\leqslant N_c\leqslant n$. Indeed, its small-tolerance exponents are constant multiples of $N_cx^2$ for $D_U=1$, $N_c(x/\log(2+1/x))^2$ for $D_U=2$, and $N_cx^{D_U}$ for $D_U>2$. At the specified tolerance these grow at least as $\log^4n$, $\log^2n$, and $\log^{2D_U}n$, respectively. Bounded support supplies the exponential-moment assumption. A coupling pushed through $\Phi_c$ multiplies its cost by at most the Lipschitz constant of $\Phi_c$. For $D_U=0$, each conditional observed law is a point mass and its conditional empirical error is zero. Binomial concentration also gives $\sum_c|N_c/n-p_c|\leqslant C\sqrt{\log n/n}$ with probability at least $1-O(n^{-4})$. Couple common categorical-component masses by their conditional couplings and unmatched masses arbitrarily within the observed support. After a union bound over the finitely many categories, \[ W(P_n^{\theta^*},P^{\theta^*})\leqslant\sum_c\min\{p_c,N_c/n\}W((\Phi_c)_\#\mu_c,(\Phi_c)_\#(\mu_c)_{N_c})+\frac{B_V}{2}\sum_c|N_c/n-p_c|\leqslant t_n, \] \[ t_n=C_2n^{-1/\max\{2,D_U\}}\log^2n, \] with probability at least $1-O(n^{-3})$. Terms with zero common mass are omitted. Lemma~\ref{lemma:sinkhorn_approx} and the triangle inequality give, on the combined event, \[ \sup_{\eta\in\mathcal A_n}|h_n(\eta)-g(\theta_\eta)|\leqslant2(1+\log(nm_n))\lambda_n+Cr_n+t_n\leqslant s_n. \] The event has probability at least $1-O(n^{-3}+m_n^{-3})$.  We construct a feasible approximation to the true model. For a structural function $f:[-K,K]^m\rightarrow\mathbb R^{m'}$ with $m\geqslant1$, divide every coordinate into $R$ intervals of length $h=2K/R$ and triangulate each cell into simplices with successive vertices $v_0,v_1=v_0+he_{\pi(1)},\ldots,v_m=v_{m-1}+he_{\pi(m)}$. Let $I_hf$ interpolate the vertex values affinely. Its derivative column in direction $e_{\pi(j)}$ is $(f(v_j)-f(v_{j-1}))/h$, of $1$-norm at most $L_f$. Subdividing a segment at simplex boundaries and summing these derivative bounds proves $\operatorname{Lip}(I_hf)\leqslant L_f$. With barycentric coordinates $a_j$, \[ \|I_hf(x)-f(x)\|\leqslant\sum_{j=0}^ma_j\|f(v_j)-f(x)\|\leqslant L_fmh. \] Convex interpolation preserves the bound $K$ for continuous outputs and preserves the simplex for categorical propensities. Its nodal basis functions are translates and rescalings of \[ \phi(z)=\max\left\{0,\min\left(\{1+z_k,1-z_k:k\in[m]\}\cup\{1+z_k-z_l:k,l\in[m]\}\right)\right\}. \] On each simplex of a nodal star this function is affine, equals one at the central vertex, and equals zero at its other vertices. Hence $I_hf(x)=\sum_v f(v)\phi((x-v)/h)$. Compute each minimum by a binary tree using $\min(a,b)=a-\max\{a-b,0\}$. Each term has width $O(m^2)$ and depth $O(1+\log m)$. Parallelizing $O(R^m)$ terms and summing their outputs gives the required fixed-dimensional depth and width $O(R^m)$. Coordinatewise input clipping is a contraction and preserves the Lipschitz bound. Taking $R$ proportional to $W_{0,n}^{1/m}$ gives error $O(W_{0,n}^{-1/m})$. A function with $m=0$ is constant and represented exactly. For categorical functions take $q=I_hf$; it is nonnegative and normalized, and its normalized Lipschitz constant equals its original one. Thus these approximants satisfy the categorical restrictions. Continuous output clipping preserves the error bound and cannot increase the Lipschitz constant.  For each normalized latent support component measure $\mu_i$, let $\psi_i:[0,1]^{q_i}\rightarrow C_i$ be its Lipschitz chart. For $q_i>0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:holder_curve} applied to its pullback measure gives a curve $\gamma_i:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1]^{q_i}$ of Holder exponent $1/q_i$ with that pullback law. Theorem 2(b) of \cite{Yarotsky2018OptimalAO} applied to its coordinates gives first-block uniform error $O(L_{1,n}^{-2/q_i})$ and, applied to the Lipschitz coordinates of $\psi_i$, gives second-block error $O(L_{2,n}^{-2/q_i})$. Parallelize coordinate networks and clip first-block outputs to their input cubes. Their widths fit the specified budgets. Lemma~\ref{lemma:push-forward_err} bounds the resulting component Wasserstein error by $O(L_{1,n}^{-2/q_i}+L_{2,n}^{-2/q_i})$. For $q_i=0$, use the exact constant component. Lemma~\ref{lemma:combin_err} bounds the hard-selected mixture error by the weighted component errors. Couple positive-temperature and hard Gumbel weights, retaining identical independent bounded component outputs $v_i$. Then \[ \left\|\sum_i(X_i^{\tau_n}-X_i^0)v_i\right\|\leqslant C\|X^{\tau_n}-X^0\|_1. \] Lemma~\ref{lemma:gumbel_err} bounds the additional error by $O(\tau_n(1-\log\tau_n))$ for sufficiently large $n$. Output truncation cannot increase the latent error because the true latents lie in $[-K,K]^{d_j^U}$ and truncation contracts distance to every point of this cube. Choose the latent generators independently. Summing their marginal errors and the structural errors gives a representation $\eta_n\in\mathcal A_n$ satisfying \[ a_n=d(\theta^*,\theta_{\eta_n})\leqslant O\left(W_{0,n}^{-1/d_{\max}^{\text{in}}}+\sum_{i=1}^2L_{i,n}^{-2/d_{\max}^U}+\tau_n(1-\log\tau_n)\right). \] Choose the constant in $\epsilon_n$ so that $C_ga_n\leqslant\epsilon_n$. On the combined sampling event, \[ h_n(\eta_n)\leqslant g(\theta_{\eta_n})+s_n\leqslant C_ga_n+s_n\leqslant\epsilon_n+s_n=\alpha_n. \] Thus the optimization is feasible. Since $m_n=\Omega(n)$, the same event has probability at least $1-O(n^{-2})$ and gives \[ W(P_n^{\mathcal M^*},P^{\mathcal M^*})\leqslant O(\alpha_n),\qquad\sup_{\eta\in\mathcal A_n}W(P_{m_n}^\eta,P^{\theta_\eta})\leqslant O(\alpha_n). \] For every feasible representation $\eta$, Lemma~\ref{lemma:sinkhorn_approx} and the empirical constraint give \[ W(P_n^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V),P_{m_n}^\eta(\boldsymbol V))\leqslant S_{\lambda_n}(P_n^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V),P_{m_n}^\eta(\boldsymbol V))+2(1+\log(nm_n))\lambda_n\leqslant O(\alpha_n), \] since the regularization term is included in $s_n\leqslant\alpha_n$.     On the same sampling event, the triangle inequality gives, for every feasible representation $\eta$, \begin{align*} w_\eta&=W(P^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V),P^{\theta_\eta}(\boldsymbol V))\\ &\leqslant W(P^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V),P_n^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V))+W(P_n^{\mathcal M^*}(\boldsymbol V),P_{m_n}^\eta(\boldsymbol V))+W(P_{m_n}^\eta(\boldsymbol V),P^{\theta_\eta}(\boldsymbol V))\\ &\leqslant O(\alpha_n). \end{align*}     All feasible models have bounded continuous structural functions and normalized categorical propensity functions with Lipschitz constant at most $\hat L_f$. The true model also belongs to the corresponding bounded Lipschitz class. Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:Lip_ATE} to the true model and each feasible model, using their common unconfounded graph and the overlap assumption of the true model. Write \[ b_\eta(t)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal M^*}[Y(t)]-\mathbb E_{\mathcal M^{\theta_\eta}}[Y(t)],\qquad r(t)=\frac{d\mu_T}{dP}(t). \] With the fixed constants $C_W,L_y$ supplied by Proposition~\ref{prop:Lip_ATE} at Lipschitz bound $\hat L_f$, it gives \[ \int_{t_1}^{t_2}b_\eta(t)^2P(dt)\leqslant\frac{2C_W}{\delta}w_\eta+2L_y^2w_\eta^2P([t_1,t_2]). \] Absolute continuity and Cauchy--Schwarz therefore give \begin{align*} \left|\mathbb E_{t\sim\mu_T}\mathbb E_{\mathcal M^{\theta_\eta}}[Y(t)]-F_*\right| &=\left|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}b_\eta(t)r(t)P(dt)\right|\\ &\leqslant\left(\int_{t_1}^{t_2}b_\eta(t)^2P(dt)\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{t_1}^{t_2}r(t)^2P(dt)\right)^{1/2}\\ &\leqslant A_T\left(\frac{2C_W}{\delta}w_\eta+2L_y^2w_\eta^2P([t_1,t_2])\right)^{1/2}\\ &\leqslant C\sqrt{\alpha_n}. \end{align*} For the last inequality, the growth assumptions imply $\alpha_n\rightarrow0$, so $\alpha_n\leqslant1$ eventually and $w_\eta^2=O(\alpha_n^2)=O(\alpha_n)$; all other factors are fixed. The bound is uniform over feasible representations. Feasibility was established on the same event, so every feasible objective lies in $[F_*-C\sqrt{\alpha_n},F_*+C\sqrt{\alpha_n}]$. Taking its infimum proves $|F_n-F_*|\leqslant C\sqrt{\alpha_n}$, whether or not the infimum is attained. The event has probability at least $1-O(n^{-2})$.
- why: The inherited-assumption lint warnings are dismissed: independence, both categorical clauses, all three Lipschitz/boundedness clauses, both support clauses, both lower-bound clauses, and the latent-law premise are inherited through \cref{thm:consistency}. The regularized-notation warning is also dismissed: the corollary uses the stated Sinkhorn comparison without independently invoking $W_{1,\lambda}$. The triangle inequality requires three distances: population to observational empirical law, observational empirical to candidate empirical law, and candidate empirical to population law. The printed middle term repeats the population distance, but substituting the empirical distance bounded immediately above closes this proof slip. The substantive defect is the final invocation of Proposition \ref{prop:Lip_ATE}: it controls the squared response difference integrated against $P$, whereas $F_n-F_*$ averages against $\mu_T=\text{Unif}([t_1,t_2])$. No stated hypothesis relates these measures. The counterexample satisfies the referenced assumptions but makes the displayed rate false.

### `prop:equivalent-g-constrianed` (`proof.tex:600-602`)

- as printed: \label{prop:equivalent_g_constrianed} Suppose that \cref{assump:independence_u} and \cref{assump:categorical_rv} hold, given any SCM $\mathcal{M} $ with causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ and latent variables $\boldsymbol{U}$, we can construct a canonical SCM $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ of the form (\ref{eq:structure_equation}) by merging the latent variables in $\boldsymbol{U}$ such that $\mathcal{M}$ and $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ produce the same intervention results. Besides, functions in $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ have the same smoothness as $\mathcal{M}$.
- corrected: Suppose that \cref{assump:independence_u} and \cref{assump:categorical_rv} hold, given any SCM $\mathcal{M} $ with causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ and latent variables $\boldsymbol{U}$, we can construct a canonical SCM $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ of the form (\ref{eq:structure_equation}) by merging the latent variables in $\boldsymbol{U}$ such that $\mathcal{M}$ and $\hat{\mathcal{M}}$ produce the same intervention results. Besides, the continuous structural functions in $\hat{\mathcal M}$ have the same smoothness as those in $\mathcal M$. The categorical functions in $\hat{\mathcal M}$ have the smoothness of the normalized propensity functions $f_i/\|f_i\|_1$: normalization preserves differentiability order and local Lipschitz regularity wherever $\|f_i\|_1>0$, and coordinate regrouping preserves any global Lipschitz regularity these normalized functions possess.

Assumption \ref{assump:Lip_and_bounded} explicitly identifies normalized propensity coordinates with conditional category probabilities.

No covariance or moment convention is imposed in the SCM definition.
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-190`: In the categorical branch of (\ref{eq:structure_equation}), zero coordinates of the normalized nonnegative vector $f_i(x)$ are allowed and are evaluated using $\log 0=-\infty$. — pins reading of def:eq-structure-equation: The canonical definition normalizes categorical propensity vectors, and Assumption \ref{assump:Lip_and_bounded} identifies their coordinates with conditional probabilities. The probability-simplex convention permits zero probabilities, so strict positivity would impose an additional restriction.
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-191`: Under $\boldsymbol{T}=\boldsymbol{t}$, every unreplaced equation is evaluated in topological order at the intervened values of its parents, with the original latent law unchanged; for canonical categorical nodes the unreplaced equation is the categorical branch of (\ref{eq:structure_equation}). — pins reading of def:intervention: The intervention passage explicitly calls these the structural equations of the intervened model and defines the resulting variables as their values under intervention. The later canonical definition specifies the categorical form of those structural equations.
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-c0174608`: The categorical generation formula requires $f_i(x)\in[0,\infty)^{n_i}$ and $\|f_i(x)\|_1>0$ on its structural input domain. — pins reading of prop:equivalent-g-constrianed: stated by the repair
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-c356d336`: A zero categorical coordinate has extended logarithm $\log0=-\infty$. — pins reading of prop:equivalent-g-constrianed: stated by the repair
- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] Let $\boldsymbol G=\{G_{V_i}:V_i\text{ is categorical}\}$. By \cref{assump:independence_u} and \cref{assump:categorical_rv}, the remaining latent variables $U_1,\ldots,U_{n_U}$ and the Gumbel coordinates are independent. For a categorical variable, put $s_i(x)=\|f_i(x)\|_1$ and $\pi_i(x)=f_i(x)/s_i(x)$. The categorical generation assumption requires nonnegative coordinates and $s_i(x)>0$ on its structural input domain. For positive coordinates, \[ \log\pi_{i,j}(x)=\log f_{i,j}(x)-\log s_i(x). \] The subtracted term is common to every coordinate, so replacing $f_i$ by $\pi_i$ leaves its Gumbel argmax unchanged. Zero coordinates remain zero and have extended logarithm $-\infty$. Thus this replacement preserves the categorical structural output for every input and the normalized vector belongs to the probability simplex.  Let $D_1,\ldots,D_{n_C}$ be the maximal $C^2$-components. For a non-Gumbel latent variable define $I(U_k)=\{V_j:U_k\in\boldsymbol U_{V_j}\}$. Independence implies that every nonempty $I(U_k)$ is a bidirected clique, so it is contained in a maximal $C^2$-component. Assign $U_k$ to one such component, choosing one when there is more than one choice. Unused latent variables may be assigned arbitrarily. Let $\hat U_C$ be the tuple of variables assigned to $C$; for an empty tuple use a constant latent variable. Disjoint tuples are independent. Their coordinate projections recover the original joint law of the non-Gumbel latent variables, and they are independent of $\boldsymbol G$.  For each $V_i$, supply all $\hat U_C$ with $V_i\in C$ as canonical inputs. Project these tuples onto the original inputs $\boldsymbol U_{V_i}$ and ignore the other coordinates. Define its continuous function by applying $f_i$ to these projected inputs and its categorical function by applying $\pi_i$. Together with the unchanged parent relations and Gumbel noise, these are exactly the normalized structural equations in (\ref{eq:structure_equation}). Every original bidirected edge is generated by a shared original latent variable and remains present after that variable is assigned to a component containing both endpoints. Every newly declared shared tuple has its affected vertices inside its clique $C$, so it introduces no edge outside the original graph. Hence the canonical causal graph is $\mathcal G$.  Couple each tuple with its original coordinates and retain the same Gumbel variables. Under any intervention, the treated variables agree by construction. In a topological order, suppose all parents of the next untreated variable agree. Its projected latent inputs agree; its continuous structural function is unchanged, or its categorical argmax agrees by the normalization identity. Its value therefore agrees as well. Induction over this order proves equality of all observed variables under every intervention, and hence equality of their intervention laws.  Coordinate projections preserve differentiability order and are $1$-Lipschitz for the $1$-norm, so they preserve global Lipschitz constants of the functions to which they are applied. Continuous functions therefore retain their original regularity, and categorical functions retain the regularity of $\pi_i$. To verify the normalization claims, if $f_i$ is differentiable to a given order and $s_i>0$, the quotient by the positive differentiable function $s_i$ has that same differentiability order. If $f_i$ is locally Lipschitz, fix an input where $s_i>0$ and a neighborhood on which $s_i\geqslant a>0$. For two points $x,y$ in that neighborhood, nonnegativity gives $|s_i(x)-s_i(y)|\leqslant\|f_i(x)-f_i(y)\|$, and \[ \left\|\frac{f_i(x)}{s_i(x)}-\frac{f_i(y)}{s_i(y)}\right\| \leqslant\frac{\|f_i(x)-f_i(y)\|}{s_i(x)}+\frac{|s_i(x)-s_i(y)|}{s_i(x)} \leqslant\frac{2}{a}\|f_i(x)-f_i(y)\|. \] This proves local Lipschitz regularity of the normalized propensity. If that propensity is globally Lipschitz, composing it with the coordinate projections retains its global bound, completing the stated regularity conclusions.
- why: ``Same smoothness'' could mean only the same differentiability order, or preservation of the original regularity through coordinate regrouping, including global Lipschitz regularity. The proof's explicit retention of the original functions determines the latter reading. (a) The original categorical assumption permits unnormalized functions, but the printed construction retains them unchanged while claiming the normalized canonical form. (b) Normalizing those functions does not generally preserve global Lipschitz regularity, so normalization is not a harmless missing line under the proposition's unrestricted domains.

### `prop:holder-curve` (`proof.tex:1238-1240`)

- as printed: \label{prop:holder_curve} Let $ \lambda $ be the Lebesgue measure on $ [ 0,1]$. Given any probability measure $ \mathbb{P}$ that satisfies \cref{assumption:lower_bound}, there exists a continuous curve $ \gamma : [0,1]\rightarrow \text{supp}(\mathbb{P})$ such that $\gamma _{\#} \lambda =\mathbb{P}$. Furthermore, if $d \geqslant 1$, $\gamma$ is $ 1/d$-Hölder continuous.
- corrected: statement unchanged
- no longer uses `lem:holder-curve-shchepin-theorem-1`

- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] \label{proof:holder_curve} Without loss of generality, we can assume that $ \mathbb{P}$ is supported on $[0,1]^d$,  vanishes at the boundary and $\mathbb{P}(B) \geqslant C_1\lambda(B)$ for some constant $C_1>0$ and all measurable sets $B\in[0,1]^d$. Suppose we have proven the conclusion for this case. By \cref{assumption:lower_bound}, there exists $ f\in \mathcal{H}([0,1]^{d},K) \cap \mathcal{F}_L([0,1]^{d},K)$ such that $f^{-1}_{\#} \mathbb{P}$ satisfies these conditions. There exists continuous function $\gamma$ such that $f^{-1}_{\#}\mathbb{P}=\gamma_{\#}\lambda$, which implies $\mathbb{P} = (f\circ\gamma)_{\#}\lambda$. In particular, if $\gamma$ is $1/d$-Holder continuous, $f\circ\gamma$ is also $1/d$-Holder continuous because $f$ is Lipschitz continuous.   When $d = 0$, the constant map satisfies the requirement. We focus on the case $d\geqslant 1$ in the following. The proof is to modify the construction of the Hilbert space-filling curve. By changing the velocity of the curve, the push-forward measure of the Hilbert space-filling curve can simulate a great number of distributions. We use $ \lambda $ to represent the Lebesgue measure $ [0,1] $. \par     We prove the cube case by first constructing a uniform Hilbert curve and then changing its parameter. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]^d$ and retain $\lambda$ for Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$. The cube probability measure satisfies $\mathbb P\geqslant C_1\lambda_d$, so $0<C_1\leqslant1$.   \textbf{Step 1: Define partition.}    First, we construct a sequence of partitions that has the property (*) recursively. Let $ \mathcal{C}_{0} =\left\{[ 0,1]^{d}\right\}$. Construct $\mathcal C_{n+1}$ by bisecting every coordinate interval of every cell of $\mathcal C_n$ at its midpoint. Label each parent's $2^d$ children by $i_{n+1}\in\{0,\ldots,2^d-1\}$ and append this label to the parent's address. Induction gives \[ \mathcal C_n=\left\{\prod_{r=1}^d[a_r2^{-n},(a_r+1)2^{-n}]:a_r\in\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}\right\}. \] These closed cube collections have the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal C_n$ is obtained by cutting $[0,1]^d$ by planes parallel to the coordinate planes. \item Every parent is the union of its $2^d$ children, and \[ C_{i_1,\ldots,i_n}=\bigcup_{i_{n+1}=0}^{2^d-1}C_{i_1,\ldots,i_n,i_{n+1}},\qquad \text{diam}(C_{i_1,\ldots,i_n,i_{n+1}})=\frac12\text{diam}(C_{i_1,\ldots,i_n}). \] \item For every $C\in\mathcal C_n$, $\lambda_d(\partial C)=0$ and $\lambda_d(C)=2^{-nd}$. \end{enumerate} The midpoint halves cover each coordinate interval, so their products cover the parent. Each child edge is half the corresponding parent edge, proving the diameter equality. Every level-$n$ edge has length $2^{-n}$, giving the displayed volume. Each boundary is a finite union of coordinate faces, each having a singleton in one coordinate and hence zero product Lebesgue measure. Thus these collections satisfy property (*), and every level-$n$ cell has $1$-norm diameter $d2^{-n}$. \par\textbf{Step 2: Construct Hilbert Curve.} By Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert}, the standard dyadic collections $\mathcal C_n$ admit orderings $O_n$ satisfying the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item If $(j-1)2^d<i\leqslant j2^d$, the first $n$ digits of $O_{n+1}(i)$ are the same as $O_n(j)$. \item Consecutive level-$n$ cubes share a full coordinate face of dimension $d-1$. \end{enumerate} Let $ \mathcal{I}_{0} =\{[ 0,1]\}$, we define $ \mathcal{I}_{n}$ recursively. For $n\geqslant1$, define \[ I_{O_n(i)}=[(i-1)2^{-nd},i2^{-nd}],\qquad 1\leqslant i\leqslant2^{nd},\qquad \mathcal I_n=\{I_{O_n(i)}:1\leqslant i\leqslant2^{nd}\}. \] Every assigned interval has length $2^{-nd}=\lambda_d(C_{O_n(i)})$. By the prefix conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lemma:hilbert}, the children of the $i$th level-$n$ cube have precisely the indices $(i-1)2^d+1,\ldots,i2^d$ at level $n+1$. Their intervals are consecutive, with first left endpoint $(i-1)2^d2^{-(n+1)d}=(i-1)2^{-nd}$ and last right endpoint $i2^d2^{-(n+1)d}=i2^{-nd}$. Their union therefore equals $I_{O_n(i)}$. The level-one intervals likewise cover $[0,1]$. The child lengths sum to $2^d2^{-(n+1)d}=2^{-nd}$; the child cube volumes have the same sum, with common faces of zero $\lambda_d$-measure. Consequently, for $n\geqslant1$ and $1\leqslant i\leqslant2^{nd}$, \begin{equation} |I_{O_n(i)}|=\lambda_d(C_{O_n(i)})=\sum_{j=(i-1)2^d+1}^{i2^d}\lambda_d(C_{O_{n+1}(j)})=\sum_{j=(i-1)2^d+1}^{i2^d}|I_{O_{n+1}(j)}|.\label{eq:sum_I} \end{equation}\par    Construct a continuous polygonal curve $H_n$ on these intervals: its initial and final points are the centers of the first and last cubes, and at each internal interval endpoint its value is a point in the common face of the two successive cubes. On each interval interpolate linearly between its assigned endpoint values. Convexity places that segment inside its assigned cube. For a parameter at an interval endpoint, both incident cubes contain the assigned value.  The nesting of the orderings implies that for $m\geqslant n$, $H_m(t)$ and $H_n(t)$ lie in one common level-$n$ closed cube. At interval endpoints choose the incident cube to the right, except at $t=1$, where the last cube is chosen. Consequently \[ \sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|H_m(t)-H_n(t)\|\leqslant d2^{-n}. \] The curves converge uniformly to a continuous map $H:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1]^d$, and $H$ maps every assigned level-$n$ interval into its assigned cube.  Let $0\leqslant u<v\leqslant1$, and choose $n\geqslant0$ with $2^{-(n+1)d}<v-u\leqslant2^{-nd}$. The two parameters lie in the same or successive level-$n$ intervals. The corresponding cubes coincide or share a face. Their union has $1$-norm diameter at most $2d2^{-n}$. Thus \[ \|H(v)-H(u)\|\leqslant2d2^{-n}\leqslant4d(v-u)^{1/d}. \] For any continuous scalar function $\varphi$ on the cube, choose the center $z_{n,i}$ of each level-$n$ cube. Both \[ \int_0^1\varphi(H(t))\,dt \quad\text{and}\quad \int_{[0,1]^d}\varphi(x)\,d\lambda_d(x) \] differ from $\sum_i2^{-nd}\varphi(z_{n,i})$ by at most the modulus of continuity of $\varphi$ at $d2^{-n}$. Letting $n\rightarrow\infty$ proves $H_{\#}\lambda=\lambda_d$. The compact image of $H$ therefore contains the support of $\lambda_d$, which is the entire cube; hence $H$ is surjective.  For each $x\in[0,1]^d$, define $s(x)=\min\{t:H(t)=x\}$. The fiber is a nonempty compact set. Moreover, $\{x:s(x)\leqslant a\}=H([0,a])$ is compact for every $a\in[0,1]$, so $s$ is Borel measurable and $H\circ s$ is the identity. The measure $\mathbb P-C_1\lambda_d$ is nonnegative and has mass $1-C_1$. Define the probability measure on the interval \[ \rho=C_1\lambda+s_{\#}(\mathbb P-C_1\lambda_d). \] It satisfies $\rho\geqslant C_1\lambda$ and \[ H_{\#}\rho=C_1\lambda_d+(H\circ s)_{\#}(\mathbb P-C_1\lambda_d)=\mathbb P. \] This construction allows atoms in $\rho$ and in $\mathbb P$.  Put $A(x)=\rho([0,x])$ and define $Q(0)=0$ and \[ Q(t)=\inf\{x\in[0,1]:A(x)\geqslant t\},\qquad 0<t\leqslant1. \] The domination of $\rho$ gives positive mass to every nonempty open interval, so $Q(1)=1$. Right continuity of $A$ gives, for $t>0$, the equivalence $Q(t)\leqslant x$ if and only if $t\leqslant A(x)$. Therefore $\lambda\{t:Q(t)\leqslant x\}=A(x)$, which proves $Q_{\#}\lambda=\rho$.  If $u<v$ and $Q(u)<Q(v)$, take $Q(u)<a<b<Q(v)$. The quantile definition gives $A(a)\geqslant u$ and $A(b)<v$, also when $u=0$ or $v=1$. Hence \[ C_1(b-a)\leqslant\rho((a,b])=A(b)-A(a)\leqslant v-u. \] Letting $a\downarrow Q(u)$ and $b\uparrow Q(v)$ yields $Q(v)-Q(u)\leqslant C_1^{-1}(v-u)$. If $Q(u)=Q(v)$ this bound is immediate. Thus $Q$ is Lipschitz and continuous. The cube curve $\zeta=H\circ Q$ satisfies \[ \zeta_{\#}\lambda=H_{\#}\rho=\mathbb P, \qquad \|\zeta(v)-\zeta(u)\|\leqslant4dC_1^{-1/d}|v-u|^{1/d}. \] For a measure on the original compact set $K$, apply this construction to $(f^{-1})_{\#}\mathbb P$ and take $\gamma=f\circ\zeta$. Then $\gamma_{\#}\lambda=\mathbb P$, and the Lipschitz property of $f$ preserves the exponent $1/d$. Since the domination assumption and the homeomorphism imply $\operatorname{supp}(\mathbb P)=K$, this curve has the asserted codomain.
- why: the step its proof takes from [Shchepin2010OnHM, Theorem 1] (lem:holder-curve-shchepin-theorem-1) does not hold as the proof uses it: The partition definition prints a parent-smaller-than-child inequality, whereas the subsequent construction and uniform convergence argument determine child contraction. Under that reading, two citation hypotheses still fail. (a) The interval partitions need not be developments: the host assumptions allow interior atoms, whose corresponding intervals never shrink. (b) Even for atom-free admissible measures, the printed identity $\text{diam}(\mathcal I_k)=\text{gap}(\mathcal I_k)$ is false, and the uniform comparison required by Shchepin need not hold. Maximum interval length is controlled by maximum cell mass, while a gap between disjoint intervals can be the mass of a much smaller intervening cell. The lower domination assumption supplies no uniform upper bound on their ratio.

### `lem:hilbert` (`proof.tex:1249-1255`)

- as printed: \label{lemma:hilbert} Given a sequence of partitions of the unit cube $ \{\mathcal{C}_{n}\}$ that has property (*), there exist a ordering for each partition $ \mathcal{C}_{n}$, i.e., $$ O_{n} :\left\{1,\cdots ,2^{nd}\right\}\rightarrow \left\{\overline{i_{1} i_{2} \cdots i_{n}} :i_{j} =0,\cdots ,2^{d} -1\right\},$$ such that the following two conclusions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item If $ ( j-1) \cdotp 2^{d} < i\leqslant j\cdotp 2^{d}$, the first $ n$ digits of $ O_{n+1}( i)$ are the same as $ O_{n}( j)$. \item Adjacent cubes in the ordering intersect, i.e., $ C_{O_{n}( i)} \cap C_{O_{n}( i+1)} \neq \emptyset $. Furthermore, $ C_{O_{n}( i)} \cap C_{O_{n}( i+1)}$ is a $d-1$ dimensional cube. \end{enumerate}
- corrected: Given a sequence of partitions of the unit cube $\{\mathcal C_n\}$ that has property (*), suppose that, when $d\geqslant1$, $\mathcal C_n$ is the standard dyadic grid of closed cubes \[ \mathcal C_n=\left\{\prod_{r=1}^d[a_r2^{-n},(a_r+1)2^{-n}]:a_r\in\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}\right\}. \] There exists an ordering for each partition $\mathcal C_n$, i.e., \[ O_n:\{1,\ldots,2^{nd}\}\longrightarrow\{\overline{i_1\cdots i_n}:i_j=0,\ldots,2^d-1\}, \] such that the following two conclusions hold. \begin{enumerate} \item If $ ( j-1) \cdotp 2^{d} < i\leqslant j\cdotp 2^{d}$, the first $ n$ digits of $ O_{n+1}( i)$ are the same as $ O_{n}( j)$. \item Adjacent cubes in the ordering intersect, i.e., $ C_{O_{n}( i)} \cap C_{O_{n}( i+1)} \neq \emptyset $. Furthermore, $ C_{O_{n}( i)} \cap C_{O_{n}( i+1)}$ is a $d-1$ dimensional cube. \end{enumerate}
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-0bcb2cef`: The assertion about adjacent cubes is quantified over $i$ satisfying $1\leqslant i<2^{nd}$. — pins reading of lem:hilbert: stated by the repair
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-8cc0dba5`: For every $n$, the cells of $\mathcal C_n$ are closed coordinate boxes covering $[0,1]^d$; a cell may have zero side lengths. — pins reading of def:hilbert-partitions: stated by the repair
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-99ac9bb3`: For distinct cells $C,C'\in\mathcal C_n$, the partition condition is $\operatorname{int}(C)\cap\operatorname{int}(C')=\emptyset$, with interiors taken in $\mathbb R^d$. — pins reading of def:hilbert-partitions: stated by the repair
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-c85b9186`: Each $O_n$ is a bijection. — pins reading of lem:hilbert: stated by the repair
- side condition added by the confirming referee `ass:pin-fix-e896f793`: The cells of $\mathcal C_n$ are closed and may share boundaries. — pins reading of lem:hilbert: stated by the repair
- proof change: For $d=0$, every partition has its single point as its only cell. Choose the unique ordering; the first conclusion holds and there are no adjacent pairs. For $d\geqslant1$, use the recursive Hilbert ordering on the dyadic lattice described in Section 2 of \cite{hamiltonCompactHilbertIndices2007}. That construction visits every cell once, visits all the children of a cell consecutively before moving to another cell, and joins successive cells across a coordinate face. Label each child by its position among the $2^d$ children of its parent, and define $O_n(i)$ to be the resulting address of the $i$th cell at level $n$. Visiting every cell once makes $O_n$ a bijection. Completing the children of the $j$th parent before visiting the next parent places precisely the indices $(j-1)2^d+1,\ldots,j2^d$ in that parent, so their addresses have prefix $O_n(j)$. Successive dyadic lattice cells differ by one unit in exactly one coordinate and agree in the other coordinates. Their closed cubes therefore intersect in the full common face, which has dimension $d-1$ and side length $2^{-n}$. This proves both conclusions.
- why: The terms ``partition'' and ``cube'' could mean disjoint cells and equal-sided cubes, or closed coordinate boxes with shared boundaries. The preparation and construction in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:holder_curve} determine the latter reading. Under it, property (*) permits refinement patterns for which the claimed nested face-adjacent orderings do not exist. The cited source constructs Hilbert orderings on dyadic lattices and does not establish this generalization.
