- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] Let $ \boldsymbol{V} = \{ X,T,Y\} $ be the covariate, treatment and outcome respectively. $ T$ is a binary variable. Let structure equations of causal model $ \mathcal{M}_{\delta }$ be  \begin{align*} X & =\begin{cases} -1 & ,\text{w.p.} \ 1/2\\ 0 & ,\text{w.p.} \ 1/4\\ \delta  & ,\text{w.p.} \ 1/4, \end{cases}\\ P( T=1|X=x) & =\begin{cases} 1/2 & ,x=-1\ \text{or} \ 0,\\ 3/4 & ,x=\delta , \end{cases}\\ Y & =\begin{cases} T+U_{y} & ,X< 0\\ X/\delta +U_{y} & ,X\geqslant 0 \end{cases} \end{align*}where all latent variables are independent and $ U_{y}$ is mean-zero noise. The distribution of $ \mathcal{M}_{\delta }$ is  \begin{align*} P_{X,T,Y}( 0,1,y) =p_{U_{y}}( y) /8, & \ P_{X,T,Y}( 0,0,y) =p_{U_{y}}( y) /8\\ P_{X,T,Y}( \delta ,1,y) =3p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /16, & \ P_{X,T,Y}( \delta ,0,y) =p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /16.\\ P_{X,T,Y}( -1,1,y) =p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /4, & P_{X,T,Y}( -1,0,y) =p_{U_{y}}( y) /4. \end{align*} As $ \delta \rightarrow 0$, distribution of $ \mathcal{M}_{\delta }\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{M}^*$, where structure equations of $ \mathcal{M}^*$ are  \begin{align*} P( U_{1} =1) =3/5,P(U_{1} =0) =2/5 & ,P( U_{2} =1) =1/3,P( U_{1} =0) =2/3,\\ X & =\begin{cases} -1 & ,\text{w.p.} \ 1/2,\\ 0 & ,\text{w.p.} \ 1/2, \end{cases}\\ P( T=1|X=x) & \ =\begin{cases} 1/2 & ,x=-1,\\ 5/8 & ,x=0, \end{cases}\\ Y & \ =\begin{cases} T+U_{y} & ,X=-1,\\ U_{1} +U_{y} & ,X=0,T=1,\\ U_{2} +U_{y} & ,X=0,T=0, \end{cases} \end{align*} where $ U_1,U_2,U_y $ are independent. The distribution of $ \mathcal{M}^*$ is  \begin{align*} P_{X,T,Y}( 0,1,y) & \ =p_{U_{y}}( y) /8+3p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /16,\\ P_{X,T,Y}( 0,0,y) & =p_{U_{y}}( y) /8+p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /16,\\ P_{X,T,Y}( -1,1,y) & =p_{U_{y}}( y-1) /4,\\ P_{X,T,Y}( -1,0,y) & =p_{U_{y}}( y) /4. \end{align*} Choose $U_y=0$ almost surely. Generate $X$ by $X=U_X$, where $P(U_X=-1)=P(U_X=0)=1/2$, independently of $U_1,U_2$ and the categorical Gumbel variables. Every non-Gumbel latent law, including any vector formed by merging latents affecting the same observed variable, now has finite support. For such a law $\mathbb P$, write its support components as $C_i=\{a_i\}$ and put $\mu_i=\mathbb P|_{C_i}/\mathbb P(C_i)$. The map $f:[0,1]^0\rightarrow C_i$ sending the unique point to $a_i$ is a Lipschitz homeomorphism. If $\lambda_0$ denotes the probability measure on $[0,1]^0$, then for every measurable $B\subset[0,1]^0$, \[ \mu_i(f(B))=\lambda_0(B). \] Thus each normalized component law satisfies Assumption~\ref{assumption:lower_bound} with $d=0$ and $C_f=1$; its boundary requirement applies only when $d>0$. These singleton components also verify Assumption~\ref{assump:support}. All displayed structural inputs range over finite sets. Their structural and normalized propensity maps have Lipschitz extensions: form the finite Cartesian grid of their input coordinate values, retain the prescribed values at the specified inputs, and assign bounded values at the remaining vertices, using probability vectors for propensity maps. Interpolate multilinearly on each grid cell and clamp each input coordinate to the grid's range. This preserves the prescribed values and the probability simplex. Each cell has finite coordinate slopes; taking their maximum and subdividing a line segment at cell boundaries gives a finite global Lipschitz constant. Choose $L_f$ to bound these finitely many constants. The resulting observed variables and non-Gumbel latent variables are bounded, so a finite $K$ exists. Independence and categorical generation hold by construction. Hence $\mathcal M^*$ satisfies Assumptions \ref{assump:independence_u}-\ref{assumption:lower_bound}. Some calculation gives $ W( P^{\mathcal{M}^*}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\mathcal{M}_{\delta }}(\boldsymbol{V})) \leqslant \delta /2$. It is easy to calculate the ATE of the two models.  \begin{align*} \text{ATE}_{\mathcal{M}^*} = 19/30, & \ \text{ATE}_{\mathcal{M}_{\delta }} = 1/2. \end{align*}
- why: [F2.5 reviewer] [statement-wrong] The requirement to satisfy Assumption lower_bound does not settle whole-latent-law versus normalized-component-law regularity; Lean selects the latter.

### `prop:convg-opt` (`proof.tex:1605-1631`)

- as printed: \label{prop:convg_opt} Given a metric space $ (M,d) $ and sets $ \Theta_1\subset\Theta_2\cdots\subset\Theta_n\subset\cdots\subset \Theta_\infty \subset M$, where $\Theta_\infty = \overline{\cup_{n=1}^\infty \Theta_n}$ , positive sequences $ \{\epsilon_{n}\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}},\{\delta_{n}\}_{n\in \mathbb{N}}$ such that $ \lim _{n\rightarrow \infty } \epsilon _{n}=\lim _{n\rightarrow \infty }\tau_n=\lim _{n\rightarrow \infty } \delta_{n} =0$ and continuous functions $ f,g_{n} :\Theta_\infty \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, suppose that \begin{enumerate} \item $\Theta_\infty$ is compact. \item $g_n$ satisfies \begin{equation} \label{eq:aprox_lip} \|g_n(\theta_1) - g_n(\theta_2)\| \leqslant L_g d(\theta_1,\theta_2) + \tau_n, \quad \forall \theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta \end{equation} and $ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_\infty}\|g_{n}(\theta) - g(\theta)\|\leqslant \delta_n, g_n \geqslant 0$. \item There exists a compact subset $ \tilde{\Theta}_\infty \subset \Theta_\infty $ such that for any $\theta_0 \in \tilde{\Theta}_\infty$, there exists $\theta \in\Theta_n$ such that $ d(\theta,\theta_0 )\leqslant \epsilon_n.$ \end{enumerate} Consider the following optimization problems: \begin{align} \min_{\theta \in \Theta_n } & f( \theta ) , \notag\\ s.t. &\ g_{n}( \theta ) \leqslant L_g\epsilon_{n} + \delta_n, \label{eq:opt_n} \end{align} \begin{align} \min_{\theta \in \Theta_\infty } & f( \theta ) ,\notag\\ s.t. &\ g( \theta ) = 0. \label{eq:opt*} \end{align} and \begin{align} \min_{\theta \in \tilde{\Theta}_\infty } & f( \theta ) ,\notag\\ s.t. &\ g( \theta ) = 0. \label{eq:opt*_sub} \end{align} We assume that the feasible region of (\ref{eq:opt*}) and (\ref{eq:opt*_sub}) are nonempty. Let $ f_{n}^{*}, f^*, \tilde{f}^* $ be the minimal of (\ref{eq:opt_n}), (\ref{eq:opt*}) and (\ref{eq:opt*_sub}) respectively. Then, $ [\liminf _{k\rightarrow \infty } f_{n}^{*}, \limsup_{k\rightarrow \infty } f_{n}^{*}] \subset [f^{*}, \tilde{f}^*]$.

If the uniform error is infinite, the asserted bound holds in the extended nonnegative reals.     Combining (\ref{eq:first_term}) and (\ref{eq:second_term}) bounds the difference of expectations by $LW(\mu,\hat\mu)+d_2\|F-\hat F\|_\infty$ for every scalar $1$-Lipschitz function $g$. Taking the supremum over these functions gives the asserted bound for $W(F_{\#}\mu,\hat F_{\#}\hat\mu)$.

If any $W(\mu_k,\hat\mu_k)=\infty$, the inequality holds in the extended nonnegative reals. Otherwise, for any $\epsilon>0$ and every $k\in[n]$, choose a probability coupling $\pi_k$ of $\mu_k$ and $\hat\mu_k$ such that \begin{equation*} \mathbb E_{(X_k,Y_k)\sim\pi_k}[\|X_k-Y_k\|_1]\leqslant W(\mu_k,\hat\mu_k)+\epsilon. \end{equation*} Such a coupling exists by the definition of the finite infimum defining $W$. The marginal laws of $X$ and $Y$ are respectively $\mu$ and $\hat\mu$, because the coordinate pairs are independent and have the prescribed marginal laws. Thus this construction is a coupling of the product measures. The product $1$-norm is the sum of the coordinate $1$-norms, so \begin{align*} W(\mu,\hat\mu) &\leqslant\mathbb E_{\pi_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\pi_n}[\|X-Y\|]\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E_{(X_k,Y_k)\sim\pi_k}[\|X_k-Y_k\|_1]\\ &\leqslant\sum_{k=1}^n W(\mu_k,\hat\mu_k)+n\epsilon. \end{align*} Letting $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves the result.

Let $\mu ^{0}$ be the distribution of $X^{0} =\lim _{\tau \rightarrow 0} X^{\tau } =\left( X_{1}^{0} ,\cdots ,X_{n}^{0}\right)$. Then, \begin{equation*} W\left( \mu ^{\tau } ,\mu ^{0}\right) \leqslant 2( n-1) \tau -2n( n-1) e^{-1} \tau \log \tau . \end{equation*}

### `lem:sinkhorn-approx` (`proof.tex:2030-2039`)

- as printed: \label{lemma:sinkhorn_approx} For any $ \mu \in \Delta _{n} ,\nu \in \Delta _{m}$ and $ \lambda >0$, we have \begin{align*} 0\leqslant W_{1,\lambda}( \mu ,\nu ) -W( \mu ,\nu ) & \leqslant (\log( mn) +1) \lambda, \end{align*} where $ W_{1,\lambda}(\cdot,\cdot) $ is the entropy regularized Wasserstein-1 distance. - proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] The transportation polytope is nonempty and compact, and both objectives are continuous under $0\log0=0$, so their minima exist. Let $T^*$ minimize the unregularized transport cost and let $T_\lambda$ minimize the regularized objective. Since $h(T)\geqslant0$ for every probability plan, \[ W_{1,\lambda}(\mu,\nu)\leqslant\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}T^*_{ij}-\lambda h(T^*)\leqslant W(\mu,\nu). \] Also $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}(T_\lambda)_{ij}\geqslant W(\mu,\nu)$. It follows that \begin{align}\label{eq:err_reg_wass} -\lambda\max_{T\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}h(T)\leqslant W_{1,\lambda}(\mu,\nu)-W(\mu,\nu)\leqslant0. \end{align} Since $ T_{ij} \in [ 0,1]$ and $ f( x) =-x\log x$ is concave, we have  \begin{align*} h( T) = & -nm\cdot \frac{1}{nm}\sum _{i,j=1}^{n,m} T_{ij}\log T_{ij} +1.\\  & \leqslant -nm\cdot \left(\frac{1}{nm}\sum _{i,j=1}^{n,m} T_{ij}\right)\log\left(\frac{1}{nm}\sum _{i,j=1}^{n,m} T_{ij}\right) +1\\  & =1+\log( nm) . \end{align*} By definition of Sinkhorn distance,  \begin{align*} S_{\lambda }( \mu ,\nu ) & = W_{1,\lambda }( \mu ,\nu ) -W_{1,\lambda }( \mu ,\mu )/2 -W_{1,\lambda }( \nu ,\nu )/2 . \end{align*} Let $a=W_{1,\lambda}(\mu,\nu)-W(\mu,\nu)$, $b=W_{1,\lambda}(\mu,\mu)$, and $c=W_{1,\lambda}(\nu,\nu)$. The self-transport Wasserstein costs are zero. By (\ref{eq:err_reg_wass}) and the entropy calculation, \[ |a|\leqslant(1+\log(nm))\lambda,\quad |b|\leqslant(1+2\log n)\lambda,\quad |c|\leqslant(1+2\log m)\lambda. \] Consequently \begin{align*} |S_\lambda(\mu,\nu)-W(\mu,\nu)| &=|a-b/2-c/2|\\ &\leqslant|a|+|b|/2+|c|/2\\ &\leqslant2(1+\log(nm))\lambda. \end{align*}

### `lem:sup-wasserstein` (`proof.tex:2061-2067`)

- as printed: \label{lemma:sup_wasserstein} Given a measure $ \mu $ on $ \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and a real function class $ \mathcal{F}$ with output dimension $ d$, suppose that the pseudo-dimension of $ \mathcal{F}$ is less than $ d_{\mathcal{F}} < \infty $ and there exists $K>0$ such that $ |f( x) |\leqslant K,\forall f\in \mathcal{F} ,x\in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$, then with probability at least $ 1-\exp\left( O\left( \delta ^{-d}\log\left( \delta ^{-1}\right) +d_{\mathcal{F}}\log \epsilon ^{-1} -n\epsilon ^{2}\right)\right)$, \begin{align*} \sup _{f\in \mathcal{F}} W( f_{\#} \mu ,f_{\#} \mu _{n}) & \leqslant \delta +\epsilon \end{align*} for all $ \delta ,\epsilon >0$, where $ \mu _{n}$ is the empirical distribution of $ \mu $.
- corrected: Given a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^{d'}$ and a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable functions $f:\mathbb R^{d'}\rightarrow\mathbb R^d$, suppose that each scalar coordinate class $\mathcal F_j=\{x\mapsto f_j(x):f\in\mathcal F\}$, $j\in[d]$, has pseudo-dimension less than $d_{\mathcal F}<\infty$ and there exists $K>0$ such that $\|f(x)\|_\infty\leqslant K$ for all $f\in\mathcal F$ and $x\in\mathbb R^{d'}$. Suppose in addition that there are a standard Borel space $T$ and a jointly Borel map $G:T\times\mathbb R^{d'}\rightarrow[-K,K]^d$ such that $\mathcal F=\{G(t,\cdot):t\in T\}$. There are positive constants $C,c$ depending only on $d,K$ such that, with probability at least \[ 1-\exp\left(C\left((1+\delta^{-d})\log(2+\delta^{-1})+d_{\mathcal F}\log(2+\epsilon^{-1})\right)-cn\epsilon^2\right), \] \begin{align*} \sup_{f\in\mathcal F}W(f_{\#}\mu,f_{\#}\mu_n)\leqslant\delta+\epsilon \end{align*} for all $\delta,\epsilon>0$, where $\mu_n$ is the empirical distribution of $\mu$.

- proof change: the printed proof, revised step by step] The empty class satisfies the uniform assertion vacuously, so assume $T\ne\varnothing$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent observations with law $\mu$. By the dual formulation of Wasserstein distance, \begin{align*} \sup_{f\in\mathcal F}W(f_{\#}\mu,f_{\#}\mu_n) =\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left(\mathbb E_{X\sim\mu_n}h(f(X))-\mathbb E_{X\sim\mu}h(f(X))\right), \end{align*} where \[ \mathcal H=\{h:[-K,K]^d\rightarrow\mathbb R:h(0)=0,\ |h(x)-h(y)|\leqslant\|x-y\|\}. \] Every such $h$ takes values in $[-dK,dK]$. Retain the unnormalized empirical covering number \begin{align*} \mathcal N_1(r,\mathcal F,N)=\sup_{x_1,\ldots,x_N}\mathcal N\left(r,\{(f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_N)):f\in\mathcal F\},\|\cdotp\|_1\right), \end{align*} where the $1$-norm on the evaluation vector sums over all sample points and output coordinates.  With the uniform norm, $\mathcal H$ is closed, uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on the compact cube, hence is a compact metric space by Arzela--Ascoli. Evaluation $(h,y)\mapsto h(y)$ is continuous: its increment is bounded by $\|h-h'\|_\infty+\|y-y'\|$. Consequently $(t,h,x)\mapsto h(G(t,x))$ is jointly Borel on $T\times\mathcal H\times\mathbb R^{d'}$. Its bounded population integral is Borel in $(t,h)$: this holds for indicators of measurable rectangles, is preserved by bounded monotone limits and linear combinations, and extends to bounded Borel functions by the monotone class theorem. Every strict deviation event is the projection of a Borel set from this standard Borel parameter space and is therefore analytic and universally measurable; weak supremum events are countable intersections of strict ones. The same reasoning applies to two samples and finite coordinate swaps. All probabilities below are thus defined in the completion of the sample law. Obviously, if $ h$ is 1-Lipschitz,  \begin{align*} \mathcal{N}_{1}( \epsilon ,h\circ \mathcal{F} ,n) & \leqslant \mathcal{N}_{1}( \epsilon ,\mathcal{F} ,n) . \end{align*} Put $v=\lfloor d_{\mathcal F}\rfloor$. Each coordinate class has pseudo-dimension at most $v$. Normalize its range by $f_j\mapsto(f_j+K)/(2K)$. Applying Theorem 18.4 of \cite{anthony1999neural} in its averaged empirical metric, and then undoing the normalization, bounds a scalar unnormalized cover of radius $r/(2d)$ on $N$ points by \[ e(v+1)\left(2+\frac{8eKdN}{r}\right)^v. \] The additional $2$ allows radii beyond the normalized unit range. Take the product of these $d$ covers. For every product ball meeting the evaluation vectors of $\mathcal F$, choose one such vector as its center. Two vectors in that product ball differ by at most $r/d$ in each scalar unnormalized metric, hence by at most $r$ in the summed vector metric. Thus \[ \mathcal N_1(r,\mathcal F,N)\leqslant\left[e(v+1)\left(2+\frac{8eKdN}{r}\right)^v\right]^d. \] This exhibits both sample-size and range scaling.  Fix $h\in\mathcal H$, and define \[ a_f(x)=\frac{h(f(x))+dK}{2dK},\qquad z_f(x)=\sqrt{a_f(x)}. \] Both functions take values in $[0,1]$. On $N$ points, the inequality $|\sqrt a-\sqrt b|\leqslant\sqrt{|a-b|}$ and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality give \[ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|z_f(x_i)-z_g(x_i)|\leqslant\left(\frac{1}{2dKN}\sum_{i=1}^N\|f(x_i)-g(x_i)\|\right)^{1/2}. \] Consequently an unnormalized vector cover of radius $2dKNr^2$ gives an averaged scalar cover of the class $\{z_f:f\in\mathcal F\}$ of radius $r$, whose cardinality is at most \[ \left[e(v+1)(2+4e/r^2)^v\right]^d. \] By Theorem 17.1 in \cite{anthony1999neural}, with its standing measurability condition, let $X$ and $T_0$ be standard Borel spaces, let $g:T_0\times X\rightarrow[0,1]$ be jointly Borel, and put $\mathcal G=\{g(t,\cdot):t\in T_0\}\ne\varnothing$. For every Borel probability distribution $P$ on $X\times[0,1]$, every $0<\zeta<1$ and every positive integer $m$, \[ P^m\left\{\text{some }t\in T_0\text{ has }\left|\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P}(g(t,x)-y)^2-\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(g(t,x_i)-y_i)^2\right|\geqslant\zeta\right\} \leqslant4\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(\zeta/16,\mathcal G,2m)\exp(-\zeta^2m/32). \] Here the draws are independent, the probability is taken in the completed sample law, and $\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}$ uses the averaged empirical metric. For the present class, $(t,x)\mapsto\sqrt{(h(G(t,x))+dK)/(2dK)}$ is jointly Borel, since $h$ is continuous and the square root is continuous on $[0,1]$. Its parameter space is the same standard Borel space $T$, and its constant-response input law is $\mu\otimes\delta_0$. Apply this form of Theorem 17.1 to the class with response identically zero. Its squared loss is $z_f^2=a_f$. For $0<\epsilon<2dK$, put $\eta=\epsilon/(2dK)$ and use the averaged cover at radius $\eta/16$ on $2n$ points. The theorem gives \[ \mathbb P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|(\mu_n-\mu)(h\circ f)|>\epsilon\right) \leqslant4\left[e(v+1)(2+1024e/\eta^2)^v\right]^d\exp(-n\eta^2/32). \] Since $v\leqslant d_{\mathcal F}$ and $\log(v+1)\leqslant v$, the logarithm of the right-hand side is bounded by $C_0+C_1d_{\mathcal F}\log(2+\epsilon^{-1})-c_1n\epsilon^2$, with constants depending only on $d,K$. If $\epsilon\geqslant2dK$, the deviation is deterministically at most $2dK$, and the desired deviation bound is immediate. Let $\mathcal H_\delta$ be a finite $\delta/2$-net of $\mathcal H$ in the uniform norm. Such a net has \[ \log|\mathcal H_\delta|\leqslant C_2(1+\delta^{-d})\log(2+\delta^{-1}), \] where $C_2$ depends only on $d,K$. To see this, take a grid in $[-K,K]^d$ with $1$-norm mesh at most $\delta/8$ and at most $(1+C_3/\delta)^d$ points. Quantize the values of $h$ at these points into bins of width at most $\delta/8$ in $[-dK,dK]$. There are at most $2+C_4/\delta$ bins at each point. Choose one member of $\mathcal H$ from each nonempty quantization pattern. Two functions with the same pattern differ by at most $\delta/8$ at grid points and by at most $3\delta/8$ everywhere, using their Lipschitz bounds and a nearest grid point. These representatives form the required net. Counting patterns gives the displayed entropy bound. Apply the fixed-$h$ concentration bound to every $h\in\mathcal H_\delta$ and take a union bound. For $0<\epsilon<2dK$, after enlarging a constant depending only on $d,K$, \[ \mathbb P\left(\sup_{h\in\mathcal H_\delta,f\in\mathcal F}(\mu_n-\mu)(h\circ f)>\epsilon\right) \leqslant\exp\left(C\left((1+\delta^{-d})\log(2+\delta^{-1})+d_{\mathcal F}\log(2+\epsilon^{-1})\right)-cn\epsilon^2\right). \] For every $h\in\mathcal H$, choose $\tilde h\in\mathcal H_\delta$ with $\|h-\tilde h\|_\infty\leqslant\delta/2$. Since $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ are probability measures, \[ |(\mu_n-\mu)((h-\tilde h)\circ f)|\leqslant\delta. \] Therefore \[ \sup_{h\in\mathcal H,f\in\mathcal F}(\mu_n-\mu)(h\circ f) \leqslant\delta+\sup_{\tilde h\in\mathcal H_\delta,f\in\mathcal F}(\mu_n-\mu)(\tilde h\circ f). \] The dual formula yields the stated Wasserstein bound. If $\epsilon\geqslant2dK$, both push-forward measures are supported in a set of $1$-norm diameter $2dK$, so their Wasserstein distance is at most $2dK\leqslant\delta+\epsilon$ deterministically. This completes the proof for all positive $\delta,\epsilon$.
- why: the step its proof takes from [anthony1999neural, Theorems 18.4 and 17.1] (lem:sup-wasserstein-anthony-theorems) does not hold as the proof uses it: (a) For vector-valued $\mathcal F$, its pseudo-dimension could mean $\max_{j\in[d]}\operatorname{Pdim}(\{f_j:f\in\mathcal F\})$ or $\operatorname{Pdim}(\{(x,j)\mapsto f_j(x):f\in\mathcal F\})$. These impose different bounds, and neither the paper nor the scalar cited theorem specifies the choice. The dual formulation does determine that $h$ is scalar-valued. (b) The attributed covering inequality is false for the paper's explicitly unnormalized empirical $\ell_1$ metric: its bound omits sample-size scaling. (c) It also omits range scaling: Theorem 18.4 requires scalar functions valued in $[0,1]$, whereas the host only bounds their magnitude by arbitrary $K$. The fixed-$h$ concentration order can be recovered from Theorem 17.1 by range normalization and a square-root transformation with zero responses, but that does not validate the printed covering inequality.

## Findings withdrawn by the owner

Not errors: the paper's owner showed each finding misreads the paper. The printed statement stands, under the owner's reading (or side condition), which the formalization adopts.

- `def:relu-networks` (raised at F2.5): the owner's reading (`ass:pin-owner-3`): A network in $\mathcal{NN}_{k_1,k_2}(W,L)$ has $L$ hidden layers, each of width at most $W$, followed by the affine output layer (width at most $W$ and exactly $W$ give the same class of functions: a narrower layer is padded with zero units). The covering number $\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,S,\\|\cdot\\|_1)$ is that of the cited source (Anthony and Bartlett): the least size of a subset $C\subseteq S$ such that every point of $S$ lies at $\ell_1$ distance strictly less than $\epsilon$ from some point of $C$. — the withdrawn finding: [statement-wrong] The frozen phrase 'width W and depth L' does not distinguish exact sizes from budgets or specify whether depth counts hidden layers or includes the output layer.
- `def:lemma-sup-wasserstein-empirical-covering` (raised at F2.5): the owner's reading (`ass:pin-owner-4`): A network in $\mathcal{NN}_{k_1,k_2}(W,L)$ has $L$ hidden layers, each of width at most $W$, followed by the affine output layer (width at most $W$ and exactly $W$ give the same class of functions: a narrower layer is padded with zero units). The covering number $\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,S,\\|\cdot\\|_1)$ is that of the cited source (Anthony and Bartlett): the least size of a subset $C\subseteq S$ such that every point of $S$ lies at $\ell_1$ distance strictly less than $\epsilon$ from some point of $C$. — the withdrawn finding: [statement-wrong] The frozen definition does not specify strict versus closed covering balls or internal versus ambient centers; Lean selects strict internal covers.

def PerekrestenkoQuantizedGeneration : Sort 0 := -- @realizes s(natural-number source depth fixed by let s := 1 below; distinct from delta and delta / n)
  ∃ c : ℕ, 0 < c ∧ ∀ q : ℕ, 0 < q → ∃ A : ℝ, 1 ≤ A ∧ -- @realizes \Theta(d_i^C)(depth c * q with one multiplier c for every dimension q; the source's depth (s+3)q-s-1 = 4q-2 at s = 1)
    ∀ (d N : ℕ) (P : ProbabilityMeasure (L1Vec d))
      (S : Fin N → Set (L1Vec d)) (dC : Fin N → ℕ) (L : ℝ≥0),
      SupportFiniteComponents (P : Measure _) S →
      ComponentsLipschitzHomeomorphic S dC L →
      ∀ (i : Fin N), dC i = q →
      ∀ f : homeoClass (unitCube (dC i)) (S i), LipschitzWith L f →
      ∃ B : ℝ, 0 < B ∧ ∀ W₁ : ℕ, A * (2 : ℝ)^q ≤ W₁ → -- @realizes W_1(component width budget above the dimension-dependent threshold)
        let n : ℕ := ⌊((W₁ : ℝ) / A) ^ (1 / (q : ℝ))⌋₊ -- @realizes n(refinement floor chosen from W_1 and the dimension-only width factor A)
        let s : ℕ := 1 -- @realizes s(carrier ℕ and fixed value s = 1; source depth, distinct from quantization delta and mesh delta / n)
        let delta : ℝ := (⌈Real.sqrt q * (q + 1) * n * ((n : ℝ) - 1)⌉₊ : ℝ)⁻¹ -- @realizes \delta(prescribed quantization parameter at the pinned refinement)
        2 ≤ n ∧ A * (n : ℝ)^q ≤ W₁ ∧
        ∃ Phi : ReLUNet 1 (dC i) W₁ (c * q), -- @realizes \hat{g}_1^i(quantized component network of width W_1 and depth proportional to its positive dimension)
          (∀ l ∈ Phi.hidden, (l.output : ℝ) ≤ A * (n : ℝ)^q) ∧
          Phi.paramsQuantized (delta / n) ∧
          wasserstein1 ((ProbabilityTheory.cond (P : Measure _) (S i)).map (chartInverse f))
            ((uniformCubeLaw 1).map Phi.eval) ≤
              ENNReal.ofReal (B * (W₁ : ℝ) ^ (-(1 : ℝ) / q))
```

> By \cite[Theorem VIII.1]{perekrestenkoHighDimensionalDistributionGeneration2022a}, there exists quantized ReLu network $ \hat{g}_{1}^{i}$ of width $ W_{1}$ and depth $ \Theta( d_i^C)$ (let $ s=\frac{1}{\lceil n( n-1)\rceil }$ in \cite[Theorem VIII.1]{perekrestenkoHighDimensionalDistributionGeneration2022a}), such that \begin{equation*}
>     W\left(\left( (g_{2}^{i})^{-1}\right)_{\#} \mu _{i} ,P(\hat{g}_{1}^{i}(U_{i}))\right) \leqslant O\left( W_{1}^{-1/d_i^C}\right) ,
>     \end{equation*}
>     where $ U_{i}$ are i.i.d. uniform random variables on $ [ 0,1]$.

def YarotskyCoordinateApprox : Sort 0 :=
  ∀ d : ℕ, 0 < d → ∃ a c : ℝ, 0 < a ∧ 0 < c ∧
    ∀ (D : ℕ) (S : Set (L1Vec D)), IsCompact S →
      ∀ (f : homeoClass (unitCube d) S) (L : ℝ≥0), LipschitzWith L f →
        ∀ j : Fin D, ∀ depth : ℕ, 1 ≤ depth →
          ∃ q : ReLUNet d 1 (12*d) depth,
            ∀ x ∈ unitCube d,
              |(if hx : x ∈ unitCube d then (f ⟨x,hx⟩).val.ofLp j else 0) -
                (q.eval x).ofLp 0| ≤
                a * euclidModulus
                  (fun y => if hy : y ∈ unitCube d then (f ⟨y,hy⟩).val.ofLp j else 0)
                  (c * (depth : ℝ) ^ (-(2 : ℝ) / d))
```

def YarotskyStructuralApprox : Sort 0 :=
  ∀ d : ℕ, 0 < d → ∃ a c : ℝ, 0 < a ∧ 0 < c ∧
    ∀ (n b : ℕ) (kind : Fin n → NodeKind) (dims : Fin b → ℕ)
      (dag : Causalean.Graph.DAG (Fin n)) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
      (C : Fin b → Set (Fin n)) (M : CanonicalSCM kind dims dag G C)
      (i : Fin n) (hd : structuralInputSize M.toEuclideanSCM i = d),
      let f := fun x : L1Vec d => M.f i
        (structuralFiniteCoordinates M.toEuclideanSCM i
          (WithLp.toLp 1 (fun k => x.ofLp (Fin.cast hd k))))
      ∀ L : ℝ≥0, LipschitzOnWith L f (unitCube d) →
        ∀ j : Fin (outputDim (kind i)),
          ∀ depth : ℕ, 1 ≤ depth → ∃ q : ReLUNet d 1 (2*d+10) depth,
            ∀ x ∈ unitCube d,
              |(f x).ofLp j - (q.eval x).ofLp 0| ≤
                a * euclidModulus (fun y => (f y).ofLp j)
                  (c * (depth : ℝ) ^ (-(2 : ℝ) / d))
```

The passage of the proof:

> By \cite[Theorem 2]{Yarotsky2018OptimalAO}, part b), applied with $p=2/d_{i}^{\text{in}}$ to each output coordinate of $f_i$, which is Lipschitz continuous on the input cube by \cref{assump:Lip_and_bounded}: there are narrow fully-connected ReLU networks of constant width $2d_{i}^{\text{in}}+10$ and depth $L_0$ whose sup-norm error is at most $a\,\omega(cW^{-2/d_{i}^{\text{in}}})$, where $W$, the number of weights, grows linearly in $L_0$ at fixed width; stacking the $d_{i}^{\text{out}}$ coordinates gives, if $V_i$ is continuous, $ \| \hat{f}_{i} -f_{i} \| _{\infty } \leqslant O(L_0^{-2/d_{i}^{\text{in}}}) \leqslant O(L_0^{-2/d_{\max}^{\text{in}}}) $.

def FournierGuillinSmallDeviation : Sort 0 :=
  ∀ d : ℕ, 1 ≤ d → -- @realizes d(positive source Euclidean dimension)
    ∀ alpha gamma e : ℝ, 1 < alpha → 0 < gamma →
      ∃ C c : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ 0 < c ∧ -- @realizes C(positive source prefactor fixed before the law and sample size) -- @realizes c(positive source exponent constant fixed before the law and sample size)
        ∀ mu : ProbabilityMeasure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)), -- @realizes \mu(probability law on Euclidean space with the source two-norm)
          Integrable (fun z => Real.exp (gamma * ‖z‖ ^ alpha)) (mu : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d))) →
          (∫ z, Real.exp (gamma * ‖z‖ ^ alpha) ∂(mu : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)))) = e →
          ∀ N : ℕ, 1 ≤ N → -- @realizes n(positive IID source sample size N)
            ∀ x : ℝ, 0 < x → x ≤ 1 →
              (Measure.pi (fun _ : Fin N => (mu : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)))))
                {z | ENNReal.ofReal x ≤ wasserstein1
                  ((N : ℝ≥0∞)⁻¹ • ∑ i : Fin N, Measure.dirac (z i)) (mu : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d)))} ≤
                ENNReal.ofReal (C * Real.exp (-c * N *
                  (if d = 1 then x^2 else if d = 2 then
                    (x / Real.log (2 + x⁻¹))^2 else x^d)))
```

The passage of the proof:

> \item By definition of $ g_{n}$, 
> \begin{align*}
> |g_{n}( \theta ) -g_{n}( \theta') | & =|S_{\lambda _{n}}\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -S_{\lambda _{n}}\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta'}(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\\
>  & \leqslant |W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta'}(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |+ 4(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n}\\
>  & \leqslant W\left( P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta'}(\boldsymbol{V})\right) + 4(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n}\\
>  & \leqslant O( d( \theta  ,\theta')) +4(1+\log( nm_{n})) \lambda _{n} ,
> \end{align*}
> where we use  Lemma \ref{lemma:sinkhorn_approx} in the second inequality and triangle inequality and \cref{thm:approximation} in the third inequality. By the condition in \cref{thm:consistency}, the second term $ (1+\log( nm_{n})) \lambda _{n} \rightarrow 0 $
>  as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Therefore, (\ref{eq:aprox_lip}) is verified with $\tau_n = 4(1+\log( nm_{n})) \lambda _{n} $. 
>  
> We then verify the uniform convergence of $g_n$. By triangle inequality, 
> \begin{align*}
> |g_{n}( \theta ) -g( \theta ) | & =|S_{\lambda _{n}}\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\\
>  & \leqslant |S_{\lambda _{n}}\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\\
>  & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ +|W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |.
> \end{align*}
> By Lemma \ref{lemma:sinkhorn_approx},  $ |S_{\lambda _{n}}\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\leqslant  2(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n}$ and we get 
> \begin{align}
> |g_{n}( \theta ) -g( \theta ) | & \leqslant  2(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n} +|W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\notag\\
>  & \quad \ \ \ \ +|W\left( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) -W\left( P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) |\notag\\
>  & \leqslant  2(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n} +W\left( P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{V})\right) +W( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{V}) ,P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{V}))\notag\\
>  & \leqslant  2(\log( mn) +1) \lambda _{n} +O\left(W( P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{U}) ,P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{U})) + W\left( P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{U}) ,P^{\theta}_{m_n}(\boldsymbol{U})\right)\right) ,\label{eq:uniform_app_err}
> \end{align}
> where we use \cref{thm:approximation} in the last inequality.
> 
> We first bound $ \sup _{\theta } W\left( P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{U}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{U})\right)$ using standard VC dimension argument. Note that $ \{U_{1} ,\cdots ,U_{n_{U}}\}$ are independent. By \cref{lemma:product_err},
> \begin{equation}\label{eq:decomp_u}
>     W\left( P^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{U}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }(\boldsymbol{U})\right) \leqslant \sum _{i=1}^{n_{U}} W\left( P^{\theta }( U_{i}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }( U_{i})\right).
> \end{equation}
> By the construction in \cref{thm:wide_nn}, $ P^{\theta }( U_{i}) \sim \sum _{j\in[N_{C,i}]} p_{j}P( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) ,Z_{i,j} \sim \text{Unif}( 0,1)$, where $ f_{\theta _{i,j}}$ are neural networks with constant width and depth $ L_{1,n} + L_{2,n}$, $N_{C,i}$ is the number of connected components of $\text{supp}(P(U_i))$ and $\theta_{i,j} $ are the parameters of the neural networks. By \cref{lemma:combin_err},
> \begin{align*}
> \sup _{\theta } W\left( P^{\theta }( U_{i}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }( U_{i})\right) & \leqslant O(\max_{j\in[N_{C,j}]}\sup _{\theta _{i,j}} W(P( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) ,P_{m_{n}}( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j}))) .
> \end{align*}
> By \cite{bartlett2019nearly}, the pseudo-dimension of $ \mathcal{NN}(\Theta(1) ,L)$ is $ O\left( L^{2}\log L\right)$. By boundness of all the neural networks and \cref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} \footnote{Note that we truncate the neural network to ensure boundness in \cref{thm:consistency}. This extra truncate operation $\tilde{f} = \max\{-K,\min\{K,f\}\} $ can be viewed as two extra ReLu layers, so \cref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} is still applicable. }, with probability at least $$ 1-\exp\left( O\left( (\epsilon^{'}_{n})^{-d_{\max}^{U}}\log (\epsilon^{'}_{n})^{-1} + (L_{n,1}+L_{n,2})^{2}\log(L_{n,1}+L_{n,2})\log \epsilon _{n}^{-1} -m_{n} \epsilon _{n}^{2}\right)\right) ,$$
> the following event happens. 
> \begin{align*}
> \sup _{\theta _{i,j}} W(P( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) ,P_{m_{n}}( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) & \leqslant \epsilon _{n} +\epsilon^{'}_{n} .
> \end{align*}
> Let $$ \epsilon^{'}_{n} =m_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n} ,L_{n,i} =m_{n}^{d_{\max}^{U} /\left( 2d_{\max}^{U} +4\right)}\log m_{n} ,\epsilon _{n} =Cm_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n}$$ 
> with constant $ C >0$ sufficiently large, we get 
> \begin{align*}
> P\left(\sup _{\theta _{i,j}} W(P( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) ,P_{m_{n}}( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j}))) \leqslant O\left( m_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n}\right)\right) & \geqslant 1-O\left( m_{n}^{-2}\right) .
> \end{align*}
> As long as $ m_{n} = \Omega(n)$, the Borel-Cantelli lemma implies that almost surely, there exists $ N > 0 $ such that when $ n > N$, $ \sup _{\theta _{i,j}} W(P( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j})) ,P_{m_{n}}( f_{\theta _{i,j}}( Z_{i,j}))) \leqslant O\left( m_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n}\right)$ for all $ i,j$. Therefore, almost surely, for sufficiently large $ n$,
> \begin{align}
> \sup _{\theta } W\left( P^{\theta }( U_{i}) ,P_{m_{n}}^{\theta }( U_{i})\right) & \leqslant O\left( m_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n}\right),\label{eq:uniform_app_err2}
> \end{align}
> 
> \cite[Theorem 2]{fournier2015rate} shows that for sufficiently large $ n $, if $\delta_n = C_1 n^{-1/\max\{ d^U_{\max},2\}}\log^2(n) $, where $ C_1 >0$ is a constant, 
> \begin{align*}
> P( W( P^{\theta^*}({U}_i) ,P^{\theta^*}_{n}({U}_i))  >\delta _{n}) & \leqslant \begin{cases}
> \exp( -CC_{1}\log^2( n)) & d^U_{\max} =1,\\
> \exp\left(\frac{-CC_{1}\log^{4} (n)}{\log^2\left( 2+C_{1}^{-1} n^{1/2}\log^{-2} (n)\right)}\right) & d^U_{\max} = 2,\\
> \exp( -CC_{1}\log^{2/d^U_{\max}} (n)) & d^U_{\max} >2,
> \end{cases}
> \end{align*} 
> where $C > 0$ is a constant. Let $ C_{1}$ sufficiently large such that 
> \begin{equation*}
> P( W( P^{\theta^*}({U}_{i}) ,P^{\theta^*}_{n}({U}_{i}))  >\delta _{n}) \leqslant O\left( n^{-2}\right) .
> \end{equation*}
> Therefore, $ \sum _{n=1}^{\infty }P( W( P^{\theta^*}({U}_{i}) ,P^{\theta^*}_{n}({U}_{i}))  >\delta _{n}) < \infty .$ By Borel-Cantelli lemma, with probability 1, there exist $ N >0$ such that $ W( P^{\theta^*}({U}_{i}) ,P^{\theta^*}_{n}({U}_{i})) \leqslant \delta _{n} ,\forall n >N$. By \cref{eq:decomp_u}, with probability 1, there exist $ N >0$ such that
> \begin{equation}
>     W( P^{\theta^*}(\boldsymbol{U}) ,P^{\theta^*}_{n}(\boldsymbol{U})) \leqslant O(\delta _{n}) ,\forall n >N. \label{eq:uniform_app_err3}
> \end{equation}
> 
> Therefore, by \cref{eq:uniform_app_err,eq:uniform_app_err2,eq:uniform_app_err3}, almost surely, the following inequality holds eventually, 
> \begin{equation*}
> \sup_{\theta \in \Theta_\infty}|g_{n}( \theta ) -g( \theta ) |\leqslant O\left(\log( nm_{n})\lambda _{n} +\delta _{n} +m_{n}^{-1/\left( d_{\max}^{U} +2\right)}\log m_{n}\right) = s_n,
> \end{equation*}
> where $s_n$ is defined in \cref{thm:consistency}.

`lem:sup-wasserstein-anthony-theorem-17-1` (anthony1999neural, Theorem 17.1), invoked in the proof of `lem:sup-wasserstein`:

What Lean assumes for it: `Papers.TbsNeuralCausalPi.AnthonyBartlettSquaredLoss` (`Setup/CitedResults.lean:183`)

```lean
def AnthonyBartlettSquaredLoss : Sort 0 :=
  ∀ (X : Type) (_mX : MeasurableSpace X) [StandardBorelSpace X]
    (G : Set (X → ℝ)), G.Nonempty → BorelParametrizedClass G →
    ∀ hG : (∀ g ∈ G, Measurable g ∧ ∀ x, g x ∈ Set.Icc (0:ℝ) 1),
    ∀ P : ProbabilityMeasure (X × Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1),
      ∀ (m : ℕ), 1 ≤ m → ∀ eps : ℝ, 0 < eps → eps < 1 →
        (Measure.pi (fun _ : Fin m => (P : Measure (X × Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1)))).completion
          {z : Fin m → X × Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1 | ∃ g ∈ G,
            |(∫ xy : X × Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1, (g xy.1 - xy.2.val)^2
                ∂(P : Measure (X × Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1))) -
              (m : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ i, (g (z i).1 - (z i).2.val)^2| ≥ eps} ≤
          4 * (N1avg (eps/16) G (2*m) (fun g hg => (hG g hg).2)).toENNReal *
            ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp (-(eps^2 * m)/32))
```

The passage of the proof:

> The cited assertion used in Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} is the following restricted form of Theorem 17.1 in \cite{anthony1999neural}, with its standing measurability condition. Let $X$ and $T$ be standard Borel spaces, let $g:T\times X\rightarrow[0,1]$ be jointly Borel, and put $\mathcal G=\{g(t,\cdot):t\in T\}\ne\varnothing$. For every Borel probability distribution $P$ on $X\times[0,1]$, every $0<\epsilon<1$ and every positive integer $m$,
> \[
> P^m\left\{\text{some }t\in T\text{ has }\left|\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P}(g(t,x)-y)^2-\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(g(t,x_i)-y_i)^2\right|\geqslant\epsilon\right\}
> \leqslant4\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon/16,\mathcal G,2m)\exp(-\epsilon^2m/32).
> \]
> Here the sample consists of independent draws from $P$, the probability is taken in its completion, and $\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(r,\mathcal G,N)$ is the supremum over $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ of the covering number of the evaluation vectors in the metric $N^{-1}\sum_i|u_i-v_i|$.

`lem:sup-wasserstein-anthony-theorems` (anthony1999neural, Theorem 18.4), invoked in the proof of `lem:sup-wasserstein`:

What Lean assumes for it: `Papers.TbsNeuralCausalPi.AnthonyBartlettPacking` (`Setup/CitedResults.lean:164`)

```lean
def AnthonyBartlettPacking : Sort 0 :=
  ∀ (X : Type) (G : Set (X → ℝ)), G.Nonempty →
    ∀ hG : (∀ g ∈ G, ∀ x, g x ∈ Set.Icc (0:ℝ) 1),
    ∀ v : ℕ,
      Causalean.Stat.Concentration.HasPseudoDimAtMost (fun g : G => g.val) v →
      ∀ (m : ℕ), 1 ≤ m → ∀ eps : ℝ, 0 < eps → eps ≤ 1 →
        (M1avg eps G m hG).toENNReal <
          ENNReal.ofReal (Real.exp 1 * (v+1) * (2 * Real.exp 1 / eps) ^ v)
```

The passage of the proof:

> By Theorem 18.4 in \cite{anthony1999neural}, if $\mathcal G$ is a nonempty class of functions from a set $X$ into $[0,1]$ with finite pseudo-dimension $v$, then for every $0<\epsilon\leqslant1$ and every positive integer $m$,
> \begin{align*}
> \mathcal{N}_{1}^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon,\mathcal G,m)\leqslant\mathcal{M}_{1}^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon,\mathcal G,m)<e(v+1)\left(\frac{2e}{\epsilon}\right)^{v},
> \end{align*}
> where $\mathcal{N}_{1}^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon,\mathcal G,m)$ and $\mathcal{M}_{1}^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon,\mathcal G,m)$ are the largest, over $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in X$, covering and packing numbers of $\{(g(x_1),\ldots,g(x_m)):g\in\mathcal G\}$ in the averaged metric $d_1(u,w)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m|u_i-w_i|$.

Carry each condition into its corrected statement or proof and preserve completed work. minimal patch (confirmed): corrected statement: The cited assertion used in Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} is the following restricted form of Theorem 17.1 in \cite{anthony1999neural}, with its standing measurability condition. Let $X$ and $T$ be standard Borel spaces, let $g:T\times X\rightarrow[0,1]$ be jointly Borel, and put $\mathcal G=\{g(t,\cdot):t\in T\}\ne\varnothing$. For every Borel probability distribution $P$ on $X\times[0,1]$, every $0<\epsilon<1$ and every positive integer $m$, \[ P^m\left\{\text{some }t\in T\text{ has }\left\|\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P}(g(t,x)-y)^2-\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(g(t,x_i)-y_i)^2\right\|\geqslant\epsilon\right\} \leqslant4\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon/16,\mathcal G,2m)\exp(-\epsilon^2m/32). \] Here the sample consists of independent draws from $P$, the probability is taken in its completion, and $\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(r,\mathcal G,N)$ is the supremum over $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ of the covering number of the evaluation vectors in the metric $N^{-1}\sum_i\|u_i-v_i\|$. · proof change: The cited assertion used in Lemma~\ref{lemma:sup_wasserstein} is the following restricted form of Theorem 17.1 in \cite{anthony1999neural}, with its standing measurability condition. Let $X$ and $T$ be standard Borel spaces, let $g:T\times X\rightarrow[0,1]$ be jointly Borel, and put $\mathcal G=\{g(t,\cdot):t\in T\}\ne\varnothing$. For every Borel probability distribution $P$ on $X\times[0,1]$, every $0<\epsilon<1$ and every positive integer $m$, \[ P^m\left\{\text{some }t\in T\text{ has }\left\|\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P}(g(t,x)-y)^2-\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m(g(t,x_i)-y_i)^2\right\|\geqslant\epsilon\right\} \leqslant4\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(\epsilon/16,\mathcal G,2m)\exp(-\epsilon^2m/32). \] Here the sample consists of independent draws from $P$, the probability is taken in its completion, and $\mathcal N_1^{\mathrm{avg}}(r,\mathcal G,N)$ is the supremum over $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in X$ of the covering number of the evaluation vectors in the metric $N^{-1}\sum_i\|u_i-v_i\|$. This structural domain supplies the standing measurability condition: the loss is bounded and jointly Borel, and its integral against $P$ is Borel in $t$. The latter assertion holds for indicators of measurable rectangles, is preserved by bounded monotone limits and linear combinations, and hence holds for bounded Borel functions by the monotone class theorem. Each bad event is a projection of a Borel subset of $T\times(X\times[0,1])^m$, so it is analytic and universally measurable. Replacing the sample by two independent samples or applying any of the finitely many coordinate swaps gives Borel functions on finite products and therefore the same measurability conclusion. Thus the sample and ghost-sample events used by Theorem 17.1 are measurable in the completed sample laws, and that theorem gives the displayed inequality.
